THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with
Adolphus "Doc" Cheatham

Washington, D. C.
April 1976

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
NATIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
202 347-5995
PROCEEDINGS
Born in Nashville, Tennessee. June 13, 1905. In fact it was outside of Nashville, in a little town between Nashville and Murfreesboro, but now it's called all the city of Nashville.
Uh-huh.
In other words, Nashville, Tennessee.
Now is that -- is it true that you got your nickname Doc, because there were a lot of doctors in the family.

Yes, yes. We lived in Nashville just in the (unintelligible) Mehari medical college vicinity. Just about right in that area. And when I started playing, I was playing trumpet in the Mehari Little Symphony Orchestra, which we played a little concert every first Sunday. And before the -- I guess the president of G. W. Hubbard then was the president of Mehari. And the Hubbard Hospital was named after him there. He always delivered a sermon something like that every first Sunday of the month. Some of the students, we played instruments we all had a little symphony. Played a selection before that. And neighbors -- people called me Doc like they did everybody else there.
Uh-huh, well what were you playing?
I was playing cornet.
You were?
Yes.
Because later you also took up soprano sax?
Yes, I took up soprano --
Instrument --
Later, yes.
And, now, this N. C. Davis --
That was a teacher that was brought into the little chapel where we were gathered to have a juvenile band. He was a teacher, dean of the Phillips Chapel brought this teacher in to instruct us kids --
Well his name -- what is the N. C. stand for?
Nathaniel.
Nathaniel C. Davis?

Nathaniel C. Davis, yes. He was a very famous man and he had a brother, C. M. Davis, trumpet player and he had a brother, O. B. Davis, who died in New York, he was a great drummer. And he had a sister which was a fine -- they're all a family of musicians.
Now when you were playing in this school band, what sort of music were you playing there?
Well, the first tune that we played was called, 'Action Quick Step.' It was a little march, like. See this was in the Phillips Chapel, where just the dean de-

cided to have this group, I mean the kids played and he brought in, naturally, little church songs and marches and things for us supposed to play. I guess I was about the only one who wasn't reading, but I was faking, they didn't know the difference.
Uh-huh.
We played little marches and things like that. For quite a long time, and church hymns.
Was there anyone else in that band that we would've heard of?
No, I don't think so.
Uh-huh.
Because they're all -- all of them dropped out of music, you know, except myself -- and the drummer the drummer -- no, I was the only one that continued out of the whole group.
Now your family -- we mentioned there were a lot of doctors in the family --
Yes.
How did they then feel about you taking up music?

Well, they didn't -- they didn't object. None of them objected. My father, he -- he was kind of -- little worried about it because in those days, musicians would the in Nashville he was see that -- natural, there wasn't too much going on like a street band, military band and that --
guys would drink so much -- he was afraid of that and he wanted me to -- to go through medical school also, he was very disappointed about that.
But, now see, what year are we talking about?
We're talking about 1920 and '21 --
Up to '24 --
All right, so jazz was already emerging at that time?
It was emerging at that time. But not too much around that area.
But is that when you were interested in or --
Yes, I was interested in jazz, yes.
I see. Were you listening to those early records?
Well, those that I could get, yes.
Uh-huh. Now did the family look on that as sort of low down music --
Yes, they did. Yes, they did. They didn't think too much of it, it wasn't at all thought very well of in those days.
Right. It was almost sinful, wasn't it?
Yes, absolutely, yes.
Now, then, what was your first professional job with Marion Hardy's band?

Yes, that was my first -- well I played at the Bijou Theater, there, on C-melody saxophone, after I went from soprano, I got a C-melody. And I liked that very much, in fact I liked that better than the cornet. And I guess because of the sound of it.
Hm.
And I played like in the Bijou Theater for quite a long time. On my C-melody saxophone in the pit, playing all the shows that came through there, through the TOB Association.
Uh-huh.
All the big -- all the shows you know in those times --
With this band?
With this band --
Marion Hardy?
No, that was a pit band that was headed by --
This was before Marion Hardy?
Oh, yes.
I see. Who --
This was my first -- beginning of my
first --
So, in other words, the Marion Hardy job was not your first professional job?
No, no, no. Well, I'll that. Because I wasn't getting paid at the Bijou, (I was just playing) after school hours, I'd go down and play in the pit, I wanted to see the shows --
Uh-huh.
-- and meet musicians that came through, like Joe Smith came through there with, I think, Ethel Waters at one time and then all of the show bands came through there, that were on the circuit --
Uh-huh.
-- like Sally Lewis and all of the minstrel bands and things and that was the only way I could get to hear the musicians.
Yes.
And all of the blues singers, I played with all of the blues singers on the TOB --
So this was really -- it was really a professional job?
Well I guess it was, yes, I guess it was.
Were the other musicians getting paid?
Oh, yes, it was only, I think, a
three-piece band in the pit. Piano, drums and cornet.
Uh-huh, well you were very young, then?
I was very young.
Yes.
So I just sat in there every night for quite a long time.
And what years was this?
This was in about '22 and '23.
Uh-huh.
So this was just before Bessie Smith was starting now --
Yes.
-- and Ma Rainey was actually working --
Yes, Ma Rainey was working at that time.
Did she come through there?
Yes, yes, she came through there at that time.
And, who else was in that band?

Well there was George Jefferson, who was a fine trumpet player from New Orleans, he was a Creole trumpet player, very fine -- legitimate trumpet player, I don't think he was a jazz trumpet player at all.
Uh-huh.
Pianist was Maggie [Hargraves], I think she's from Newark or something like that, she's a very fine pianist, you know playing shows and things like that she was exceptional.
Uh-huh.

The drummer, I don't know who -- I don't remember who in the heck was playing drums. I think they had one of the students from Mahari playing drums there for a while. I don't know his name. There wasn't too many drummers around in --
Did the Bijou -- that was a black theater --
Oh, yes.
Did they have these nights for white people --
Oh yes, yes.
-- midnight like rambles.
Yes, they did.
They had those -- and then the prices went up?
The prices went up, absolutely, yes.
Then, did you go from there to Marion Hardy's band?
Well, I stayed -- I stayed in the pit
until a show came through there by the name of Sunshine Sammy's Revue.
Uh-huh.
Sunshine Sammy was one of the original "Our Gang" Comedy kids. He was a black boy there and he was a very fine dancer and so his father decided to take him out with a show.
Do you remember his real name?

Right now I can't -- I probably will a little later on, I did know his name, but he and Harold Baquet Backey, which became a famous singer was on the show and a girl by the name of Glenna Cheeseman, that's about all I can remember from -- and it was a small revue and they took me out on the road with them --
Uh-huh.
-- that was my first -- I thought, well I was getting paid, I was supposed to -- getting paid.
So then -- and that was -- the leader of that band was Marion Hardy?
Marion Hardy, yes. Well, that wasn't Alabamaans, that was Marion Hardy.
Right.
Yes.
And you -- you toured with them. Were they doing tent shows?
No, they did the theaters, the TOB circuit.
This was the TOBA circuit?
Yes, uh-huh.
Now were people back as early as that time, which is the early '20's, were they referring to the TOBA as tough and on black asses?
Absolutely, yes, oh yes.
Uh-huh.
Tough or black actors, what is --
Uh-huh.

Because you see the actors mostly, they were never getting paid, see they were always in the rear, they come to Nashville they had to draw off for that week ahead of time, they were always in the rear of getting paid.
I see.
And so naturally the shows were never being paid on time.
So, where did you go with this band?
Well we went -- we played St. Louis, Chicago, Indianapolis, Memphis --
Uh-huh.
And Chicago was where the show ended because no one was getting paid --
Which theater did you play in Chicago?
The Grand, the Grand Theater. And

it broke up right there, we had a fine piano player in there, oh he did very well for himself, I can't remember his name, right now, but he did very well in Chicago, in fact, we broke up there and rather than go back to Nashville, we stayed in Chicago.
I see. Did you play at Birmingham?
No, I didn't go to Alabama --
You didn't play there?
No because the show was headed north.
Oh, so you didn't go to Atlanta, either.
I didn't go to Atlanta with that -- although I did play in Atlanta --
Later on?

No, before that. I would go to Atlanta, during the school's -- summertime, I'd go to Atlanta because I had an aunt there that was married to a Chinaman, and he had a laundry there so I used to go down in the summer and work in the laundry. And I played cornet at the 91 Theater, with Eddie Heywood Hayward's father.
Uh-huh, Eddie Heywood Hayward, Sr.
Ed Heywood Hayward, Sr.
Now the 91 was also owned by Mr. Bailey?
Yes. That was Mr. Bailey's.
Now that was a -- the better theater was the 81?
81 was the better theater, yes.
Yeah.
Oh, yes.
What was the -- really the difference, was it in --
Well the 91 seems as though it was just a makeshift theater --
Uh-huh.

-- it wasn't really built as a theater and the stage was makeshift and the show up there -- the show the dust would fly all over the stage when the dancers would dance and the place would just be full of dust. There was a lot of (unintelligible) and the element that catered to that theater was a low class of people there because they had the worst comedians and the worst blues singers in the world, at that -- what they thought.
Uh-huh.
And it was what you call a rowdy type of a theater.
Do you remember any of them?
No I don't. I'll remember the dancers some of them, they -- I remember cause whenever they'd dance the dust would fly up all over the theater, they'd throw
their feet down on the floor, the planks of the stage -- the place would be just full of dust, I don't -- because it was very comical and that's what the people liked then.
Uh-huh. What about Mr. Bailey, himself, what was he like?
Well he was -- seemed to be a very fineman. And very strict, stern. He kept everything going pretty his way.
Uh-huh.
But he was a very fine man, I thought, you know, for a theater man --
Yeah. So, okay, so then you ended up with Marion Hardy's band the Sunshine --
Sammy --
-- Sammy, show in Chicago and you left them there --
Yes.
-- and what'd you -- take up residence then in Chicago?

Yes, we -- we worked outside -- some one got us an apartment there it was a very fine lady and she put the whole band up out on the South Side, out on the South Side, and we stayed in this apartment, we had no money and our pianist, his name was Jerome Carrington, he was -- he -- he got a job with Charlie Cook, and when he would get his money

he would give (his Family) it -- gladly) a little money and it would buy food for all of us to eat. And we did that for quite a long time. And I was quite -- I guess the last one to get a gig when I was there because I was playing saxophone and cornet at that time.
Uh-huh.

And I managed to get -- through the union there was a Mrs. Hightower, she was the president of the union, then, the secretary of the union, and she helped me a lot and introduced me to Lil Armstrong and I went out with Lil Armstrong and made some gigs with her.
What year was this?
This was '26.
I see, but now weren't you with -- touring with John "Bearcat" Williams, Synco-Jazzers,
I did that, yes, --
Before?

I did that before. That was way before I went out with Hardy. But it didn't last long because that was where my uncle who was a physician at St. Louis, at the time, came to the theater and pulled me off the stage. And sent me back to school.
I see, well what kind of band was that?
That was a -- that was just a plain

loud jazz band. Johnnie Williams, he was doubling as a comedian. He was black face, he would come in the pit and play and then he would go on the stage a do comedy with a comedian. It was just playing a lot of loud jazz.
Uh-huh.
It was the type of show they had a few chorus girls.
I see, and then you were dragged off the stage --
Yes, I was sent on --
That was the end of that.
Yeah.
Okay, so getting back to -- now we're talking about 1926 --
Uh-huh.
Right.
Early '26.
Early '26, now what happened in Chicago, you were playing cornet, soprano and tenor --
Yes.
-- in those days and you joined Wynn's Al Williams* band?
Yes. I joined Al Williams* band, playing saxophone.
Uh-huh.
I had my cornet, but I didn't play too much of it -- I thought I played better cornet than I did sax, but I liked saxophone better.
Uh-huh.

At that time, cause I listened to quite a few saxophone players that I liked, like Barney Bigard, I thought he was the greatest saxophone player I ever heard in my life. At that time and so he inspired me to continue on the saxophone. At that time Louis Armstrong was with Fletcher Henderson, he was out of town, so he came back to Chicago, then I decided -- I said, well let me go to hear him so I went to hear him at the Vendome, I also heard him in Oliver's band, I think I -- quite sure I heard him in Oliver's band one year, I don't know what year that was, but that was before -- I used to go to Chicago in the summer sometimes, but I heard Louis Armstrong at the Vendome, then --
With Erskine Tate?

With Erskine Tate. Then that was my first time hearing of New Orleans musicians, I never heard of New Orleans musicians before. So then I went to hear Kneppard Freddie Kappel, and Bob Shoffner and then I got interested in that type of music and that's why I threw the saxophone away. I said the trumpet is more beautiful than saxophone and I just decided to ditch the saxophone altogether. During the time I was with Al, though, at the Dreamland I played saxophone

and then I started to play cornet, which he liked my cornet playing also, better. But he had a cornet player in the band recorded with at that time and we recall it was Ma Rainey there with Wynn Al Williams, I was playing soprano saxophone.
Uh-huh, for Paramount.
Yes.
What -- what was the Dreamland like?
Dreamland was a run down night club.
Uh-huh.

It had been a very popular place, it had run down during the time I was there, there was no business, nobody was getting paid. Bands wasn't getting paid, but we would get $5.00 or $10.00 every other night, or something. To tide us over to give the musicians, but we weren't really getting paid at all. It was rundown. Before that it was run by a fellow named Bill Bottoms.
Yes.
That was when the Dreamland was really doing well.
Well Bill Bottoms was a very dapper fellow?
Oh, yes. Oh, yes.
A ladies man?
Yes, Dreamland was really jumping at that time. But he got out of it and a fellow named Virgil

Williams took it over. So when Albert Wynn -- left the Dreamland, he left me there and Virgil Williams and -- put the band in my charge, you know. So naturally I was young, with that job, I didn't know what it was all about, so he wasn't paying, he was getting a band every night and wasn't paying the musicians. He would give me a book at the end of the night -- a ledger and he would give me maybe $20.00. And I'd sign my name at the bottom of this ledger. And I'd give the musicians -- you'd divide it up, whatever it was. And that's the way he was paying off. And I was ignorant of the fact, I didn't know what was happening. Until recently -- before the bass player, Charlie Turner died in New York, he told me, he said, you know, Virgil Williams told all the musicians in Chicago that you ran away from Chicago with the band's money. And I was surprised to hear that and he said because he showed us the books where he paid you in full, what he -- put all the money up at the top of the ledger, but I'd sign on the bottom, so he -- you know I had no receipts, I had no nothing to go by, but I don't think any of the musicians believed it.

The union didn't believe it because they knew this guy was a crook. There was only one guy believed that I ran away with some money and that was my best friend, from Nashville, the drummer, by name of Hosea Jose Duff. Now he -- I brought him to Chicago to play with me in the Dreamland and he, right to this day, believes that I ran away with the band's money.
And I did not.
And you didn't learn this till almost 50 years later?
That's right. That's right. When I was with Benny Goodman I went back to Chicago and I looked up Duff, because we went to school together --
Uh-huh.

And I called him and I wrote and no answer at all. And I went out to his house and no one was ever home. I went to his son's and no one was ever home, so he didn't want to see me at all. But he still believes that I ran away with the money. That's funny. But --
The Dreamland, about how long were you there, you long did you stay?
Well I first stayed, I guess, about three months, I guess three months.
Uh-huh.

And it was just absolutely impossible to stay there at the time. And I was losing a lot of rest, I was losing weight I was down to, I guess, about 115 pounds, because I worked a full -- 3:00 o'clock in the morning and then go hear the musicians over at the Sunset and then I'd go across the street to the -- what was the name of that night club, I forget, now. Then I'd go here -- go there. I was listening to those New Orleans musicians so much, Jimmy Noon, and all of
them till I wasn't getting any rest, and I was losing a lot of rest.
Uh-huh.
And it was, the thing, the bottom just fell out of everything in Chicago at that time.
What was Lou Armstrong doing then?
Lou was gigging, she was gigging around. Playing dances -- I mean little places, I made quite a few gigs with Lou Armstrong.
And Alberta Hunter did you play with her?
Yes, yes. And Racehorse Williams, I guess you never heard of Racehorse Williams?
No.
Racehorse Williams was a real thin girl, she was one of the greatest dancers in Chicago, at that time.
Uh-huh.

She had a -- she was real thin, but had a very pretty figure and fast as a racehorse, she'd get on the floor and she could twist and turn and she tore up everything, she was very famous then in Chicago at that time. And she and King Jones, it was King Jones, did you ever hear of King Jones?
No.

King Jones was a guy that went around all the clubs, from club to club, and he wore long full -- what do you call it -- full dress tail and his white tie and he would make announcements and would introduce all the acts in all the clubs and he tried to be British, you know?
Uh-huh.
And he was a very comical person. He was at the Dreamland at the time, and Racehorse Williams, it was the only show that they had.
Uh-huh.
When I was there.
Now was there much sitting in in those days, I mean did you to different clubs and sit in?

Yes, oh, yes. There was a lot of, but not too much over there at the Sunset, because they had their regular band. Carroll Dickerson, Cal Dixon was over there and you couldn't sit in with that band and this -- if they knew you, if you were some big shot, musician why you could go and sit in, but they would never let -- allow me to sit in at that time.
The building that housed the Sunset Glazer was owned, I believe, by Joe Glazer's mother?
That's right. Yes. that's right.
Do you remember Joe Glazer from those days?
I only knew him by name, because, you
Uh-huh.
And Earl Hines, I guess, at the Cafe Grand Terrace --
Grand Terrace, yeah.

I was listening to that band quite a lot. Well during the time I was with Al Williams, playing that -- started playing cornet, then Louis came up there to the Dreamland one day -- one afternoon and wanted me to play for him at the Vendome, sub for him, one night.
Uh-huh.

And so I did. I went down there and I was there and I don't think Louis told Erskine Tate that he was going to be out and he was sending someone, cause I set there when the band came in and no one spoke to me at all and I sat there and sat there and finally I stood up and got my horn out and got in the pit, they were rehearsing. And everybody looked and wondered what the hell, who was this guy, who was this? So I feel very embarrassed. , But, I had a lot of guts, and I had been to the Vendome, I had been going there every day and catch Louis Armstrong's show. I knew what he was playing and the tunes he was featuring that week. He did a different feature every week. I was there everyday, way up in the balcony.
Uh-huh.

Cause I was new in Chicago, so I sat in the pit and they all treated me pretty bad, there. You know, and Erskine Tate's brother, which was a trumpet player, he was very nice, he was trying to show me the score, we had to play for picture also, and they had the scores thee and everything. And it wasn't very difficult, he was showing me everything, but the only problem came was when the feature -- the band had a feature, and they were playing, at that time, "Poor Little Rich Girl." That was the feature number of the week, of Louie Armstrong.

You see when Louie was there, the minute that spotlight hit Louie, man, on the "Poor Little Rich Girl" the people were screaming so much, you couldn't hear -- you couldn't hear what he was playing, half the time. Cause he was so great. So when the spot light hit me, on "Poor Little Rich Girl," and Tate, you know, he didn't even give you a smile, he just threw his stick over there and pointed like he didn't know that.

So I jumped up and started playing and, man, the house -- the spot light and the spot light hit me and the house screamed and screamed and after awhile you could hear -- you could just measure the -- the diminishing of the screams came right down to nothing and I'm up there playing like a fool.
When they saw it was you.

They saw it was me. Well, I'll tell you, it took me years to get over that. To get over that. But I did the best I could with it. I didn't do a lousy job, but I was no Louis Armstrong. But Tate came over there, they -- they, you know, thanked me and said very nice and they say who sent you, and I told them. You know they were beginning to get friendly with me after that. Well I did quite -- I did a few of those subs over there at the Vendome, whenever he wanted me to.
Now, when you recorded with Ma Rainey, that was the first time you ever recorded?
That was my first recording, yeah.
And were you playing soprano sax?
Soprano saxophone.
Do you remember the tunes?
I do not remember the tunes. I heard them over in London, John Chilton has that record, I never heard the record, only --
What was she like?
Well, you know, she was known as the ugliest blues singer in the world. That was what she was known as.
Wasn't it the ugliest woman in show business?
Yes, ugliest show woman in show busi-
ness. I tell you I never met -- I didn't know anything about her before that and I haven't never seen her since then.
Uh-huh, so that's the only time?
That's the only time. But it was recording was very nice and she was very nice there.
Well, I heard that she was a very nice person.
Oh, yes, she was very nice, absolutely.
Uh-huh. Who else was on that recording?
Wynn's
That was Al Williams band.
Oh, it was?
Yes, Jimmy Flowers on piano and fellow named Brown on saxophone, White on trumpet -- I forget the guys -- a small band, Al and myself.
Did you ever meet Lovie Austin?
I met Lovie Austin, yes. But only met her.
You never worked with her.
Never worked with Lovie Austin at all.
Now, so you had your own band, at the Dreamland, which you had inherited?
Yes.
Actually.
Yes.
And, what was the next step, then, after that?
Well, --
Was it Tiny Parham --
Well, during the time I was there at the Dreamland I played with Tiny Parham, I think) a couple of dates.
Yes, you did a record called, 'Um Ta Da Da Da.'
That's right.
But was that recorded in St. Paul?
No that was recorded in Chicago.
Was recorded in Chicago?
Oh, yes.
The -(unintelligible) was St. Paul.
No, because I was never definitely in St. Paul with Tiny Parham.
Now was it Bob Butler who was the vocalist there, who was he?
You know I don't know -- I wouldn't even.
Or Homer Hobson?
Homer Hobson was a cornet player with Al Williams at the time. He may have been in there, he may have been with -- I don't know anyone in that band.
No, because it was -- you know, I wasn't too interested.
You didn't really work with a band then?
No I wasn't -- worked with a band. I only did --
Did sessions.
Yes.
Was that your second record session?
That must've been my second recording, yes.
And, now you went with Bobby Lee in Philadelphia?
Yes.
But what did -- did anything happen between --

No, someone sent a couple of tickets to myself and Jerry Blake. Jerry Blake, he and I were -- Nashville, you know, together, we went to school together. He was in the band in Chicago with me. And we were in this thing together. And someone sent a couple of tickets to Chicago to come to Philadelphia. It was Bobby Lee but I don't know how he learned about the two of us. That was how we got to Philadelphia from Chicago.
Who was Bobby Lee?

Bobby Lee he was a very famous out in Philadelphia. And New Jersey. He was a pianist, he looked just like a white -- very white and he had a band called Bobby Lee's Cottonpickers. And he had -- he played at the Sea Girt Inn, in Sea Girt, New Jersey every year. That's where we worked with Bobby. The first week I played at the Cinderella Inn in Philadelphia with him. That's where I joined the band. And we worked a week there and we didn't get paid, and we decided -- didn't get paid, at least I
Well, this would be around 1927?
Yes.
And was Wilbur DeParis in that band?
No Wilbur DeParis was there, he had his own band, at that time.
In Philadelphia?
In Philadelphia. He was in Atlantic City, because I didn't meet Wilbur until after I left Bobby Lee. Then I met Wilbur DeParis. In Philadelphia.
How long did you stay in Philadelphia?
Well, I stayed in Philadelphia -- must've been well I went to Atlantic City, I mean to Sea Girt with Bobby Lee. I stayed there the summer --
Uh-huh.
-- and I came back and then I joined Wilbur DeParis at the Pearl Theater. That was just about almost in -- I got into the summer.
Uh-huh.

Because Bobby Lee's band broke up after the Sea Girt Inn. And we came back and so Wilbur was there and I worked with Wilbur DeParis. At the Pearl Theater. And we played different dances around Philadelphia.
And so that wasn't very far from New York, did you -- get to New York?
Not far from New York, well not at that time. After -- the problem with Wilbur we had --
What was the problem?

Well, Wilbur was very tight with money, at that time, you know, he was very strict and he had a rooming house in Philadelphia and he kept us -- kept us there. We lived with him and he fed us and he would keep little books and he had a regular file on everybody there and if you -- whatever you ate, he'd write it down, you know. If you had an extra biscuit, he'd write it down on the paper, so that at the end of the week at the Pearl Theater, you owed him almost everything that you made. And he was paid.
Now who else was in the -- in the Wilbur DeParis band?

Well there were Bill Dillard on trumpet, and Sidney DeParis. Jerry Blake -- I don't know who else was in that band. I can't -- I don't remember who else was in -- saxophone players -- I don't. He's always had a yen for hiring
musicians that weren't popular. He liked that he could handle them better like that.
Oh, sure.
So, I don't remember exactly who else was in that band.
Well what was Philadelphia like in 1920 --
Philadelphia was very good. Very, very good. Many clubs with bands.
Uh-huh.
All over the place and shows --
Do you remember, were they still open, there was a place called Horan's?
In Philadelphia?
Yeah.
I don't remember that. No. I don't remember that.
The Madhouse?
I don't remember the Madhouse.
I guess they may have been closed by then.
Yeah.
The Standard Theater was open?
The Standard Theater was open.
Gibson?
Yes. A place called the Paradise Club.
Uh-huh.
Used to play up there, go up there all the time.
And I guess Atlantic City was jumping?
Atlantic City was jumping, oh yes.
Yeah.

I worked in Atlantic City, during the -- when I was in school. There was a fellow in Mahari there -- did a lot of work in trombone player by the name of (inaudible) Atlantic City, so he took me to Atlantic City around '25.
Uh-huh.

And he said, we'll get a band out there, so we organized a little band in Atlantic City called the Tennessee 10. And we didn't get any work. We starved to death. So I -- someone took me over to the Paradise where Charlie Johnson had his band and I went there on tenor saxophone and I played everything -- was lovely until the show, and when the show came on, I naturally couldn't read so they fired me right away. And then I went -- I was pushing chairs on the Boardwalk, hopping bells at night.
Oh, you were?
Yes. And I stayed there till I went back to school. That was just one of the crazy things that happened.
Now that was when?
That was around 1924, '25.
I see. Now when you were with Bobby Lee and you -- you worked with Wilbur and around -- somewhere around 1928, didn't you play briefly with Chick Webb?

Well you see -- yes, now when I left for -- left Wilbur, there was a fellow in New York named [Lou] Henry, he was a trombone player. He sent couple of tickets to Philadelphia, to get us out of there. Cause we didn't have any money.
Uh-huh.

And we came to New York and joined Lou Henry's band. He put us up there in his apartment on 135th Street, between Seventh and Eighth Avenues. And he got us one room with the landlady there and we worked with Lou Henry. He had a little band around here. He was playing mostly theaters, with acts.
Uh-huh.

Then, that didn't last too long, then a fellow named Lt. Tim Brymn Brown, who came back from Europe or somewhere, he was -- had a little band, a stage band and which he directed and we went to work for Lt. Tim Brymn Brown. For awhile. He had a lot of the shows and singers and things. And that didn't -- that's where Sam Wooding came in and during --
Yes, because Sam had been with

Brynn
Tim Brown.
Yes, but before Sam Wooding, I did work with Chick Webb's band. That's where I first met Johnny Hodges, and Freddy Jenkins. Well he was playing, like, dances.
Uh-huh.

You know, he play down to the hotel or some ballroom down there and I only played with him a couple of times. But he was just getting together and then that's when Sam Wooding came in and offered to take us to Europe. So I left Chick Webb and went right straight to Sam Wooding.
I see, well did anyone else leave Chick Webb with you for Sam Wooding?
Yes, Jerry Blake.
The two of you.
Yes we were together all the time up until -- until after Sam Wooding, then he went with Lionel Hampton and I went with Cab.
Now, so this was -- Sam Wooding had already been to Europe?
Oh, yes. They were back on a vacation like.
And he came back for a vacation?
Yes.
And, now was the band -- did the whole band come back or --
The whole band came back.
I see.
Oh yes, yes
So you went back over to Europe --
Uh-huh.
With -- with the whole band?
Yes.
And Tommy Ladnier was --

Yes, Tommy Ladnier was with him. I replaced a trumpet player named Edwards. I don't remember his first name. He had a brother who was a bass player with Sam Wooding. And I replaced Edwards and Jerry Blake replaced -- well I don't think he replaced anyone, I don't know whether he replaced or what not, but they took Jerry Blake and a drummer, new drummer there and a trombone player was replaced which Herbert Flemming Fleming.
I see. And what was that band like?
Sam?
Yeah.
Sam I thought had one of the greatest bands I'd ever heard. It was a very good band. We did mostly -- it was an entertaining band.
Right.
Had a lot of singing, glee clubs, you know, quartets, guys would sing in all kind of languages. Billy
Lewis, he sang in all kind of different languages. Bobby Martin and -- it was a show band.
Uh-huh.
We had Slow Kid Thompson as a comedian and Edith Wilson, and we had a few chorus girls, that went to Europe with Sam.
Yes.
Well, we opened up at the Bauphant Palace [on Zoo.] A big theater there in Berlin.
Right.
On the stage there. And --
Well, Sam, of course, already had an audience over there.
Oh, yeah, Sam -- Sam was the biggest egg I ever saw in Europe. I had never seen anybody as big as Sam.
Really?

Oh, man, we got there -- we got to Berlin there and we had [Greenley] and Drayton, famous dance team. And we right straight to the theater, we were late getting there and I'll never forget, we were in the dressing room, getting ready to go on the stage and I looked up -- out the window and saw all these waiters coming round the street, around the corner all carrying trays of food, and I didn't know what the heck was going on, they were bringing us food cause
we didn't have time to eat. And they were all coming in, all beautifully dressed and waiting on us, bringing us food at the dressing rooms to eat.
That must've been a very strange experience, coming from here with the situation the way it was here.

Oh, very -- oh yes. Yes. I thought that was the greatest thing in the world, the band. I jumped in that band and I was playing lead trumpet. That's the thing that [were] very important, money. I joined Sam Wooding as a lead trumpet player because Bobby Martin was the lead trumpet player and also did the jazz thing and it was too much for him, so I just joined the band as the lead trumpet player and then I stopped playing jazz altogether.
And --
It really broke my heart in a way but I was -- the excitement of being Europe with Sam Wooding was -- I just forgot about everything.
Uh-huh.
And I played this whole three years with Sam Wooding as lead trumpet player, all of his music and everything.
Well, wasn't -- was the band, at that time, playing things -- some of the classics?
Oh, yes.
"Tannhauser?"
"Waters of Minnetonka."
Right.

He was one of the greatest descriptive arrangers that I have ever ran into. We had a thing called the "Railroad Train." That he wrote, and you could actually hear the trains coming, he had all kinds of effects on the bandstand. That's why that man was so famous.
Uh-huh.
And he had like a radio thing he did. All announcement static with the static and everything and he was one of the greatest writers, I think I ever ran into.
So he had a lot of imagination?

Yes, he did. But he wasn't a jazz writer. AT all. He didn't approve of that, so he had the writers in the band, like Gene Sedric Sedgewick, Jerry Blake, Jerry Blake was exceptional, he was a very modern arranger at that time. If you hear Sam's album, you can hear lot of Jerry Blake's arrangements.
Uh-huh.
On the one side where the band sounds more modern than the other. I was doing some arranging too, with the band.
Oh, what did you arrange?
Well I was -- arranged two numbers

in that band, one -- the first one was called, "Carrie," which was a tune written by Edith Wilson. And that was one of our numbers we did on the stage, lot of singing and that, I arranged that. And it was a recording, I had a recording for that. And I did another arrangement on, "Weary River." Cause I was always -- wanted to improve, I never wanted to be held back to one thing. And I saw this picture that the "Weary River," I forget the name of it, was in, I saw it in Europe, and I liked the tune so well that I decided to make an arrangement on it. And I did and we recorded it in Paris. I don't know whether -- some one has it, I think a fellow I met, called me here the other day, he has that arrangement.
Uh-huh.
And that's the only two arrangements I made for the band. Cause I wasn't as fast, as either was Jerry or the rest of the guys, Cedric.
Now did you -- where else did you go in Europe. You went in Germany --
Berlin was our headquarters.
Uh-huh.
So we -- we went with the show, we went all over Germany, played Hamburg, and most of our engagements were sometimes a month --
Uh-huh.
-- to two months long. We were all
over the place, Leipzig, Dresden, Frankfurt, and hope I don't forget any -- I say Hamburg, Frankfurt, and then we went to Spain, --
To Barcelona.
Yes, we were in Madrid for almost a month or two. Then we went to the Moulin Rouge, then we went to the Florida, that's where -- Barcelona a long time there, about two, three months in Barcelona.
And you recorded while you were in Barcelona?
We recorded while we were in Barcelona.
Yes.

Yes, that's where we made our recordings, in Vienna, we were at the Moulin Rouge in Vienna, went to Constantinople, back to Hamburg and we went down to San Sebastian, Spain, we were a long time getting to Paris, because he didn't -- they wanted the band in Paris, but he didn't want to take the band to Paris, because he was afraid he would lose musicians, there, because there was -- opportunities was very good in Paris at that time, and the money was very good. So he waited till he just couldn't help himself. Last minute to take the band to Paris, now that's what happened when he took the band to Paris. I left, Jerry Blake left.
You left there?

Well, I came back to the states because I was -- listening a lot of times to this thing -- some recordings, especially Cotton-picker's Band. I fell in love with that band when I was in Europe. I heard them -- some of their recordings and I felt as though I need improvement -- I says, I'm getting stale.
Yes, I was wondering cause I asked Sam about that, you know, I asked him if he didn't feel that he was out of touch --
Uh-huh.
Being in Europe, and he said he really didn't, he had his own thing going.
Uh-huh.
I wanted to ask you about Tommy Ladnier -- Sam apparently did not think very much of him as a trumpet player.
He didn't. I don't know why, but I think Sam kept Tommy because of his name. I think that's about the only reason. Because Tom had been over there before with Sam.
I know, he was with him, originally.
Yes.
And Sam told me that he -- he really wanted Louie --
But I -- (inaudible). that's what I mean, see --
-- and Louie had gone with Fletcher
so he got Tommy instead.
Yes, because Tommy also replaced Louie in Fletcher's band.
Uh-huh.
And that was -- as far as Sam's concerned that was great jazz man. I don't know what happened to -- I don't know what happend, but I really rated Tommy up there next to Louie, I did.
Uh-huh.
At the time I heard him. I thought he was a great trumpet player and he was. Well Sam for some reason or other -- they didn't -- I don't think they got along too well.
Uh-huh.

Because Tommy was very independent type of man and he wouldn't stand for any foolishness, you know. Sam was taking -- you know, he had his way because he was underpaying me and I knew that's why I left him in Hamburg. I was doing all that playing, lead trumpet in the band and I learned that he was paying me so much under what he was paying the rest of the guys, I quit. Berlin, when he came and picked me up then he raised my salary. But Tommy I thought was one of the greatest trumpet players -- I could dig him because he had the New Orleans touch. And that's what I liked. I liked it. And Tommy and I roomed together, the whole time
we were in the band up until the time just before he left Sam in Nice. He left Sam in Nice.
You say he was a very independent man?

Oh, yes Tommy was very independent, and a good man. Very good hearted man. Tommy was a very jovial type of guy, full of fun all the time. I think the band kind of got on his nerves too, because I don't think he had an opportunity to play as much as he wanted to.
Uh-huh.
So, he wanted to get out -- get with someone where he could do more playing.
Yeah. Now when you left, you left the band in Paris, did you leave and just go straight back to New York or did you --
Yes, straight back to New York.
You didn't play in Paris?
No.
Or join anyone else?
No I just went straight to New York.
Uh-huh. And did you have to pay your own way back?
Yes.
And that was in 1929?
That was the day of the Stock Market
Crash. That was when -- that was -- our last night with Sam at this Lido Club, in Paris, I think it was the Lido, that was the night of the Stock Market Crash.
Oh, really? And so it was still 1929 when you got back?
Uh-huh.
It wasn't in the early '30's --
I guess so, yes.
That was the day of the Stock Market Crash. I'll never forget it.
How did that affect everybody?
Well, it was a shock to everybody. But things continued for awhile, I imagine, over there and then like here, they started to falling like dying out.
That obviously did not discourage you from coming back to the States?

No, I really didn't know what that meant at the time. Stock Market Crash didn't mean a thing to me, I didn't know what it meant. I was worried about -- I wanted to get back and get back in the swing and see what the guys were playing over here.
So you -- you really came back at the worst time, but you --
I came back at the worst time.
What did you do after you came back to New York --
I came --
Let me ask you first -- we haven't really gotten into your personal life. Did you -- had you married at this point?

Oh, no, no, I never married, I was only interested in music. I wasn't thinking about women, I had no girlfriends, I believe I had one girlfriend over there, but I didn't have time for that. You know I was writing and studying -- I did a lot of studying while I was there.
Uh-huh.
I studied all the time. I wanted to learn more about the trumpet.
Did you go out and listen to European music?

Yes, oh yes. I had a few instructions from trumpet players in Europe, at that time. That I heard were doing things that I wanted to know how, they were doing them. One fellow from Argentina by name of [Canaro,] he was over there with the famous Tango Band, called the [Canaro] Brothers. They had at that time the greatest tango band in the world. They were on the same bill -- same casino, Bellevue in Biarritz with Sam, we played at the same place.
Uh-huh.
Two bandstands and this trumpet player was out of sight and I would go to him everyday and get little things from him, that he was doing.
Uh-huh.
He wasn't a jazz, but he had a lot of techniques.
Yeah.
And I wanted to learn other things.
So you sailed back to New York and what happened -- I know you joined Marion Hardy's Alabamians at that point, but was that the first thing you did?
That was the first thing because --
And you joined them in New York?
Huh?
Did you join them in New York?

Yes. No, not in New York, they were at the Savoy, I went by to hear this band. Now that was a band -- there was a band who [had] -- yes, that's right, I went by the Savoy to hear this band. They had sent for me. Heard I was back.
Uh-huh.

And I went by the band to hear this band. Now there was also a band -- now I don't know whether this is the same band or not, it was headed -- that Cab was directing at that time. Now I wonder sometimes if that was

the same band, because I also heard Cab around that time and with some band, I don't know I think that was the same band, Hardy's Alabamians. They had a fellow singing with them -- when I joined them, by the name of Sonny Boy Williams. And he was imitating Cab. It could've been Sonny Boy Williams.
The original -- the old blues singer, Sonny --
Oh, no, there's another, young Sonny Boy Williams.
Uh-huh.
This guy was terrific. He was with Hardy's Alabamians when I joined them.
Uh-huh.

And so I joined Hardy, it must've been oh, let me see now. I joined Hardy's band -- I think I went to Chicago to join that band. Cause that was their headquarters. And they worked out of Chicago. Eddie Mallory was a trumpet player in the band. And Charlie Turner, bass player. That's right, I went to Chicago and joined that band. And their headquarters out of Chicago. We did one-night stands all over everywhere, Iowa and Chicago, jumping out of cars and I stayed with that band until I got an offer to go to the Cotton Pickers and that's where I wanted to be.
Now that must've been very exciting.
That was the band I wanted in the first
place, that's one reason I came back, I wanted to see if I could get with that band.
Now did you replace Langston Curl in the Cotton Picker's band?
Yes. I replaced Curl. And Bennie Carter and I went at the same time.
Now Bennie Carter was the leader of the band?
He was the leader, he replaced Don Redman at the same time I replaced Curl.
I see and you made a record with them --
Yes.
-- in -- in
Camden.
Camden in 1931.
Yes.
Which, as it turned out, was the last record --
Uh-huh.
-- they ever made.
Uh-huh.
And what was the studio like in Camden?
Well it was a very large place. It
reminded me somewhat of the old Victor place, here. That's a big, huge place. The studio was a very large room.
Uh-huh.
You could almost put a band in there and not see it. It was just like a big warehouse type -- I think it's still there.
So if you had just been a year or so later, you would never have had a chance to play with the Cotton Pickers?
That's right.
Why did they break up, were you with them when they broke up?
Oh yes, I was there. Well, money.
The depression.
They weren't paying off.
Uh-huh.

And so bass player was the first to leave, so he took all -- somehow or other he got hold to the music. He took all the music and hid it. So we didn't have anything -- we could've faked, but McKinney wanted his music. That was why the band broke up and this bass player kept the music and called Mac and says Mac you want your music you got to pay me what you owe me, and so Mac --
Blackmail?
-- yeah blackmail. And Mac says --
sent him the money so he told him the music right up in my attic so you go get it. He says, I'm gone. So he left. And that's when the band broke up. Bennie left and I left.
Uh-huh.
I came right along to New York.
Where was the band when it broke up?
In Detroit.
In Detroit?

In Detroit, yes. And I had received -- I came back here, I worked -- to New York I worked with Bennie Carter. He had a band it went into the Savoy for a short time. I recorded with him during that time.
Now, do you remember when you left the band -- when the band broke up was it -- was it 1931, or '32?
It must've been '31. Had to be '31.
'31, cause I know you made that last record, September of '31.
That's right, the same year I joined Cab. In '31. In the meantime I played with Bennie Carter at the Savoy and I also rehearsed with Fletcher Henderson.
Yes, cause there was a confusion here in what I've read up on you. It says that you were with Cab from '33 to '39, but I know that you recorded with Cab in '32, so you had to have been with Cab.
Certainly, absolutely.
At that time. Were you with Cab when he did that first movie, "Big Broadcast?"
Yes. Yes.
You were with that band?
Yes, I was with that band.
I just saw that movie recently.
Uh-huh.
Now what was that like, do you -- did you pre-record the track?

No, we went to California, I drove all the way out there without stopping, I'll never forget, I'll never get over it, either. Drove to California -- no we didn't do any pre-recording at all. That was done right on the spot.
Uh-huh. With those actors and the --
Oh, yes.
-- the microphone jumping up and down --
Yes.
-- all that nonsense.
Right on the spot.
Nonsense going on.
Uh-huh.
How was a black band treated out in Hollywood, then, I mean you were with all these white actors and it was sort of a white world?

Well, you could tell that there was an atmosphere, of you know, atmosphere wasn't too great for us. They did try to treat us very nice out there. We had no problems at all, but you could always tell, you know, it was something that you didn't feel quite comfortable.
Uh-huh.
You know, you couldn't do just what you wanted to do or go where you wanted to go.
Were you paid well for something like this?
We were paid very well for that, yes.
Uh-huh.

That's one thing I can say for Cab Calloway, he paid well, and paid on time. I don't think Cab was five minutes late paying off the band the whole time I was with him. He was just about the greatest business band leader that I ever worked for.
Uh-huh.
I can really say that for him. He was really first class. He saw that the band had everything they wanted, the best accommodations.
So you were recording quite a bit
with Cab Calloway.
Oh, yes, we made a lot of those Bettie Boop things, and all kind of shorts--
That's right you did more movie work.
Oh, yes. Did a lot of things on the train, you know, the old man of the mountain.
Were you doing these things all on that same trip out there?
No that was -- most of those were done here, while we were at the Cotton Club.
Oh, I see, I see. But when you were out in Hollywood, was it 1932, or '34?
'32, what was happening out in California, jazz-wise, were there any clubs?
There was only one club that I know of and that was out where I was -- Les Hite was playing, that was the Cotton Club.
The Sebastián --
Sebastian's Cotton Club.
Right.
That's the only place that I know of out there at the time, cause we were so busy, at the studio, we put in a lot of hours, almost 10 hours a day out there.
Uh-huh.
And you know Cab being so popular, we didn't have any days off, we got through with that we had to come right on back to work.
What about people like Bing Crosby and Eddie Lang, and those other people who were involved in that same film, did you get together with them at all?
No, we didn't. Bing was very friendly.
Uh-huh.
But the rest of people in the show, we didn't come into any contact.
You would think that someone like Eddie Lang would be very interested in --
Yes, but he wasn't.
He wasn't?
No.
And there were some other bands involved in that film, too.
There were other bands, too, we didn't come in contact with --
Or the Boswell sisters --
We didn't come in contact with them at all.
I guess they were done separately.
All separately done.
Yes. And so you -- you stayed out
there not too long. Were you performing any, or did you just go out to make the movie.
Just to make the movie.
You weren't performing at the Cotton Club or anywhere?
We did a theater date out there at -- while we were there. A week at a theater.
Uh-huh.
Almost the same time we had to double and do some -- film like some of the days we were at the theater.
Now surely when that movie came out it must've done something for the band --
Oh, yes.
-- increased the popularity?
Oh, yes. It certainly did.
Probably did more than any record, could've done.
I think so, too, yes. I think so.
And all of a sudden you were stars of --
Oh yes.
-- stage and screen.
Right, yes.
So, did you get anymore money out of
it?

Well we were paid, I thought, very well. I thought so because I tell you the truth, that was the first band that I had worked with that I was getting paid well. I thought I was getting paid well, because I'd been -- I was never paid well until I joined Cab Calloway's band. Sam Wooding paid what he paid off, but I was being underpaid the whole time I was with that band, I knew it. I was young, you know, and anxious to go to Europe, but Sam -- Cab, to me I thought I was getting very well paid.
Now you left Cab, was it '35 or '36?
I left Cab between '38 and '39. Mostly '39. '39.
Oh, I see, no, what I was thinking about, you went to Europe with Cab --
Yes.
What, in '34?
Yes, '34, we went to Europe, played there.
And where was --
Well we played the Palladium in London.
Uh-huh.
And we went to Scotland and we played in Scotland, and that's about all. Manchester.
The British Isles, so you didn't go to the Continent?
No, no.
I see. And --
And we played Paris, we had a concert in Paris at the Salle Pleyel (Unintelligible).
Uh-huh.

And we also played -- we played a couple of theaters there, we did another theater, I think it was a benefit in London, I don't remember the name of the theater. We -- the pit band at this theater, they give us a hard time before we went on, because they announced Cab's band as a benefit. The pit band started making all kinds of noise with their horns, blowing all kind of distortions that was to welcome us, the band. It was a very lousy thing they did.
Oh, you mean they were jealous?

Well, either that or they were just sort of giving us a hard time, I don't know. They just started blasting all kinds of distortions with their horns and then we came on and do it and we tore up the theater, man. Tore it up. So that gave us some sort of encouragement. We say well what those guys doing down there. So baby when that show went on and tore the theater up.
Now, when you came back, and then --
well, while you were still with Calloway, in 1936, you recorded with Putney Dandridge, right, a small band --
Uh-huh.
-- there was Teddy Wilson and who was -- it, Dixie Catlett, was it?
Big Sid Dixie Catlett.
Big Sid Allen Reuss Helen Roose and --
Yes, yes.
That was just a little side gig.
Side gigs.
Yeah.
Yes.
And -- now you then left Calloway and you went on vacation to Europe, is that right?
Yes. I went to Europe. I went to Europe, with -- I wanted to live in Europe, I just said, I want to go back. Decided to go back, I wanted to live in Europe for awhile.
Uh-huh.
And I went there and that's during the time that the war had broken out --
Before, on my way over. I went over on the America and ship blacked out before I got to Paris.
I see, so in other words, you would've
I would've stayed longer.
-- if it hadn't been for the War breaking out?
Uh-huh.
Yes.

So I had to -- a decision either to get off the boat or come back, so I got off and I -- it was a -- things were undecided then, whether the war -- one day you hear this that everything's okay, and the next day they'd say get out of Paris, next day, Embassy, we would go to the Embassy every day. So -- I stayed there. I just went to Paris and I did some gigs for the Hot Club of France, while I was -- at that time.
Oh, you did?
Yeah.
You didn't make any records?
Oh, no, not at that time. I recorded in Paris -- yes I did. I made a recording on Swing label, there for Delaunay Delaney.
Oh, you did?
Yes. I have that record.
With whom?
Just myself and a pianist and a bass and drums.
And --
And I recorded also with Eartha Kitt at the same time. I don't think those were ever released.
Eartha Kitt? In 1939?
See that was -- not -- no this one must've been in -- this was in '50, 1950.
Oh, I see.
I made quite a lot of trips to Europe. This was in '50, when I recorded with Eartha Kitt, there.
Well, we'll get to that later. Right now, you came back in October of '39?
Uh-huh.
And that's when you joined Teddy Wilson.
That's right.
And you recorded with Wilson in '39?
Uh-huh.
And with a vocalist name Jean Eldridge, right?
Yes.
Who was Jean Eldridge?
Jean Eldridge was a very fine girl. I think she would've been as big as Billie Holiday, if she had stuck with her profession. She was a great singer and she
just disappeared. I don't know what happened to Jean Eldridge after that band broke up.
And -- but in that band let's see who -- was Thelma Carpenter with that band or did she --
No, Thelma was with Coleman Hawkins band, at that time. But we were at the Golden Gate together, both bands.
Uh-huh.
She was with Coleman Hawkins.
And Al Casey --
Al Casey --
-- and Ben Webster were --
Ben Webster, yes. Carl George, Harold Hal Baker --
And where did you form with Wilson?
At the Golden Gate Ballroom, on Lennox Avenue.
I see. And so you were now living in New York?
Oh, yes.
Uh-huh. And what was -- what was that like -- there were a lot of after-hours clubs, weren't there?
Well there were after-hours clubs but not too many of them at that time, because things were very
bad in New York at that time.
Uh-huh.

And the Savoy was, naturally, trying to close the Golden Gate. I learned at that time that they wanted to buy out the Golden Gate, because it was competition. Cause the Golden Gate was taking a lot of trade away from the Savoy at that time.
Now, in the meantime, swing music has sort of taken over --
Yes.
-- and that was -- no, you were into New Orleans type of music before, so that was no problem, was it, was it just a natural transition?
Well, it was a problem, yes.
Well -- well --
It was a problem.
It was? How so?
Because it was sort of new to me, because the time with Sam, I -- was a gap inbetween what I had been doing from the Chicago era until -- then jumping back into New York at that time.
Uh-huh.
With Teddy Wilson -- Teddy Wilson just had something altogether different from any band at that time. Style of swing.
Uh-huh.
And jazz. He had a great band, it was too great, it was too good. That's why it didn't last. It was just too good.
Now, this is now 1939, you were listening to people like Louie Armstrong and Freddie Keppard?
Uh-huh.
Who were you listening to by 1939, what trumpet players were you --
Well, naturally, I was in the band with Carl George. And Harold Baker, and they were entirely new, their style of playing was entirely new to me. And I liked it very much --
Uh-huh.

-- and I felt absolutely lost, as a soloist because to get up there and play New Orleans style of solo in that band, would be -- have been out of place, entirely out of place and it wouldn't have fitted in there in the first place. It would've been entirely out of place. But you see there were a lot of other trumpet -- but New York you had other trumpet players that, you know, you were listening to at different times, like Buck Clayton.
Uh-huh.
Who was doing a lot of recording.
Yeah, the Basie band and --
And that was also a different style from New Orleans.
Uh-huh.
Yes.
But you liked the style?
I liked it, but I couldn't play it. I couldn't play the Kansas City style.
Uh-huh.
Of course, you know, we didn't do a lot of blues work in Chicago. That was mostly, what they call now, Dixieland music.
Right.
So Basie's band was built mostly around -- styled around Blues. And I wasn't too familiar with that.
Uh-huh.

And it bothered me a lot and then Harold Baker playing another different beautiful style. And Carl George, and I was just confused, I couldn't get together, I couldn't -- I didn't know what to do. So I was just there, I was just a member of the band. That's all they kept me in the band. But I was -- as a soloist I was out, finished.
Hm.
The only time that I really got a

good first opportunity is when I joined Eddie Heywood at the Cafe Society. Then, he gave me -- I was the only trumpet player and what little solos were to be played on trumpet, I did it. But not too much, but most of his music was ensemble.
That's sort of like being pushed into the pool and learning how to swim?
That's right. And I was with Eddie, recorded with Billie Holiday at that time.
Uh-huh.
Then --
But were also with Bennie Carter -- briefly
Oh, yes. Very short time because he wasn't making any money at the Savoy.
That was in 1940, right?
Yes. He gave up and he went on to California.
I see. But, we're back to 1939 and 1940, did you do a lot of Cafe Society gigs?
Yes, oh yes.
And with Billie --
Yes.
And what was Billie like?
Well, Billie, I'll tell you the truth, when I first met Billie I was very much frightened of her. Cause I heard so many things about how she'd curse out the
musicians, she'd walk out there and call you all kinds of dirty names.
Uh-huh.
You know, and I was very -- I was frightened of Billie when I first work -- first time I worked with Billie was at Kelly's Stables.
Uh-huh.

You know, little odd gigs that I played on 52nd Street. She really turned around -- she was beautiful as far as I was concerned, when you think you was satisfying her and I thought sometimes the band was satisfying her, when she finished she'd turn around and call the band a whole lot of dirty names, and go back and hide in her dressing room. And I never could understand why, I thought the band was satisfying her.
Uh-huh.
But they say she was like that. But at Cafe Society I found her to be entirely different. I found her to be very lovable person. Oh, as sweet as she could be. Always happy, you know, lovable person.
Now New York was something special, wasn't it, I mean there was a lot of -- there was -- for instance, you know James P. Johnson played a lot down at Cafe Society --
Uh-huh, yes.
And there was that stride piano, you hadn't had any of that in Chicago, had you?
That's right, no they didn't have any of that in Chicago. No.
Uh-huh.

And that was a very interesting experience, because I liked those piano cutting contests that they were having. Around here. Wow, they took my mind off everything else because I thought that was a great thing.
Who did you hear at these cutting contests?
I heard all of them. I heard James P., and Willie the Lion Smith, and Fats Waller.
Uh-huh.
And there were a few others, but I don't think they were well known at that time.
So did the audience reaction determine who won the contest?
Well, yes, I think a little comedy had a lot to do with it, too. Fats, you know, he was like a comedian, also, you know.
Uh-huh
And then there was Willie the Lion with his hat and cigar, he'd tell Fats, get up from there, you know, and that was what the people, really mostly knocked

more so by that, than then what they were playing, because they all played, you can't get away from that, they all played, but I mean it was the comedy part of it that was funny, when the cat walked it they say, get off here, who is that down there. Get off there, you know all that, then they'd just started playing and the drinks was flying and the place, you know, would be in an uproar over that sort of thing. I think all the guys were playing.
Now these cutting contests took place in places like the Cafe Society, did they?
No, Places like, when I first round the place, up on Lennox Avenue, Barrons, or some kind of place like that, Barron's, I think was the name of the place on Nest Club Glove, or something like that --
Yeah. There was also a place called Monroe's.
Monroe's oh, that's the name I was thinking about, that's where they took place.
Uh-huh, right. And the Hee-Haw?
Well, the Hee-Haw, nevermew too much about the Hee-Haw. But Monroe's that was the place where you could bet you go there and going to have some kind of cutting contest there.
And Tatum used to play at Monroe's?
Tatum, yes. Yes. Most all the piano
went by there and played, players from (unintelligible) played there.
Now how did somebody like Tatum affect you in those days? His style was --

Well I first met Tatum in Toledo, when I was with Cab. And I thought he was just amazing, I never heard a piano played like that. I thought it was amazing because it was altogether different from -- from stride piano. I thought, you know, he was -- I thought he was a classical, he sounded very classical to me, at that time.
Uh-huh.
I didn't understand too much until later on, how great he was, then I found out just how great he was. Tatum was.
It didn't really impress you too much?
It didn't at the first time, but he was so fast, you know, that I didn't get into what he was doing.
Uh-huh.
You know, the swing I wasn't used to hearing guys like Fats and the people like that, you know, with a beat --
Right.
-- and Tatum, at that time when I first heard him he didn't have a beat, but he was so fast, you
understand what I mean?
Yeah.
Took me a long time to figure him out. Cause things he was playing, just too fast for me to understand. At that time, but later on I began to dig him, what he was doing.
Uh-huh. Now what about, speaking of musicians who played differently, what about Charlie Christian when you first heard him?
Well he was -- he was -- I was so -- so astounded because I never heard a guitar played like that before.
Uh-huh.
It was marvelous thing to hear him play like that.
But you liked him right from the --
Oh, yes. Oh, yes.
Uh-huh.
Well, I had heard Django Reinhardt, too, you know, before that.
Yes, yes.
Django was very impressive, also. But Charlie had more -- altogether different feeling. Of what he was doing, than Django.
But you had heard, I assume you had
Oh, absolutely, yes.
Before that?
I knew Lonnie real well.
You knew Lonnie, personally?
Yes.
What was Lonnie like in those days?
Well --
When did you meet him, in the '20's?
I met Lonnie Johnson about in the '20's, yes.
Huh?
I met him around in the '20's. Yes.
Uh-huh.

I wasn't in his company very often, but I met him and he was a very fine fellow, I thought. Why I never, you know -- then I -- we were friendly, but I was going so much that I never ran into him too much, but I -- the last time I saw Lonnie he was in Nashville, Tennessee, I think he was a doorman there in a hotel or something --
In Nashville, Tennessee?
Uh-huh.
When was that, that must've been -- much later.
That was not too long before he died.
I was surprised when I saw him there. Because --
Because I came across Lonnie in Philadelphia, in 1958, I think it was or '59, he was working as a janitor then. And he got back into the music business, made records and --
Yes.
-- I thought he had stayed in the music business until he died, around '69, or so?
Well he was in Nashville, as doorman at a hotel there, and I don't whether he -- I think he did come back, but things weren't too, didn't go to well for him, you know.
Well, he had some -- so many come-backs, ups and downs.
Yes, yes.
But at that time, in the '20's, when you heard him, there weren't too many guitarists playing that kind of guitar --
That's right.
-- were there?
I think -- guitars -- they weren't too popular at that time.
Uh-huh.
They didn't pay too much attention to guitars, guitar was mostly used as a rhythm instrument at that
time.
Yeah.
Definitely were few. He never had an opportunity, I don't think. That he should've had. He died too early, came along a little too early, I think.

But getting back to 1940 and well, you recorded then in '41, I know with Benny Carter, Vic Dickenson, Archy Archie, Sidney Sydney DeParis and I think Maxine Sullivan was the vocalist, I guess she was big then?
Yes. Yes.
And -- so that was then -- were you with the Benny Carter band at the time you recorded in '41?
Yes, we were at the Savoy.
I see so you joined him in 1940, but you -- you were still with him in April?

Yes, we didn't stay too long up there with the band, because the work was very -- you know at that time they would like hire one week-end then maybe after a couple of weeks, we'd go up there for another couple days, something like that, because it wasn't regular. They didn't keep any band up there, that type, you know, any length of time. Cause they were more interested in bands like the Savoy Sultans, they stayed up there, because the people were jumping more to that type of band, than they were Benny Carter's band. Benny Carter's band was a little too refined for the jitterbug dancers.
So they liked a band like the Sultans and Erskine Hawkins, type of band came and stayed there.
Now did you work with Fletch, when was that, was that around '41?

Well, that was during the same time yes. I rehearsed with Fletcher with -- for quite a long time, but he didn't -- he didn't -- he was supposed to go into the Savoy, that's when he died. He didn't make it.

Uh-huh. Well Fletcher was a -- a man who would -- you know, had quite a lot of accomplishments, artistic accomplishments, but he never really -- I mean he was largely responsible for the success of the Benny Goodman band --
Yes.
-- but he never really reaped the harvest of that himself.
Never did, no. Never did.
Was he a bitter man?
No. He was a carefree type of a person, nothing seemed to bother Fletcher at all.
Uh-huh. And, when you were -- you worked with him, you were a member of the band for a little while --
I was a member of the band.
It wasn't just rehearsals, I mean you
did work.
Yes, we had a couple of jobs -- we may have played the Savoy once or twice with the band, I don't know, but it didn't last any longer than that.
I see, but you also at that time, did you go with Teddy Hill's band?
Yes, I worked with Teddy Hill's band, I think one week at the Apollo Theater. That band was working me so hard, I couldn't make it.
Now who was with the Teddy Hill band at the time?
Now the only person I can remember now, was a bass player, Dick Fullbright. He's the only person I can remember.
Oh, yeah. Dizzy wasn't with him?

Could've been -- he could've been. I don't remember, I worked so hard at that Savoy, played so many shows that I was glad that I couldn't make it any farther with that band, hardest working band I ever played with in my life.
What was so hard about it?

Well, Teddy Hill was a -- he's what we call like a slave driver, he'd keep the band blowing without regards to trumpet player's lips, they tire, you just keep them blowing all the time and screaming, you have to give a

trumpet player a little rest now and then, but there were band leaders like that that didn't realize a trumpet player had to take his horn down from his lips, you can't be screaming all night long, it's impossible and I think his band was too hard, it was one of the hardest blowing bands I've ever known.
Do you remember the first time you heard Dizzy Gillespie?
Yes.
Where was that?
At the Cotton Club.
Cause he had been with Cab Calloway, too.
Yes. He came --
After you.
-- in and sat in with the band a couple of nights at the Cotton Club, that's the first time I heard him.
Now, when was that?
That was in -- must've been in '39, early '39, because I -- he took my place, in a way, either he or Mario Bauza, they both came in the same time.
At that time he was sounding like Roy Eldridge, wasn't he?
No.
He wasn't?
I think he did play that style, but when he was sitting in with us, he was fooling around with something else, nobody understood what he was doing, and everybody was giving him hell about it.
Well, he was always sort of a clown, but -- his personality was that way.
He was fooling around with something, a different style of trumpet at that time when he joined Cab. Nobody seemed to like it, they give him -- you know, talking about it, he was working on something.
I've heard it said that Cab Calloway once told him that he didn't want any Chinese music.
Well, that could be so, I don't know, I wouldn't be surprised at all.
So when did you first realize that there was something called be-bop?
Well, after -- as soon as Charlie Parker and Dizzy got together. Then they started to -- recording that they made together. That's when I first realized that things were changing.
Uh-huh.

And everybody was getting upset about it because they thought if you couldn't play that then you're through. You couldn't play that type of jazz then you were through. That was the way everyone was feeling at that time.
So everything else was going to come to a stop.
Yeah, everything was going. And it looked like that was (what was) happening at that time.
Uh-huh.
So many trumpet players stopped and tried to play that style, lot of them just went crazy. Lost their minds.
Did you try it?
No. I couldn't -- I just couldn't find my way -- I couldn't see how to get into it.
Well you had already had to adapt to swing?
I had adapted to the New Orleans type of playing, --
Then you got into swing.
Got into swing, yeah.
And I was -- supposed this was of course a much bigger jump than going from New Orleans to swing?
Oh yes. I didn't see no way in the world that I could adopt to that because I didn't understand it.
Uh-huh.
I didn't understand it at all. I couldn't figure it out -- what was happening and I didn't like
it and it didn't make sense to me at the time.
So how does it sound to you now?
I like it.
You got used to it?
I listen to it all the time, I like it. Because you had, you see, Dizzy approved so much, because Dizzy was a good swing trumpeter in the beginning.
Yeah.
And that made a difference.
Uh-huh.

Made a big difference and you had other guys that came behind him, and that I liked too. And then it started making a lot of sense, because now Dizzy's making lot a sense, what he's playing now. I like it, I can understand it.
Well now it sounds almost traditional compared to some of the things --
That's right.
-- that are happening today.
That's right.
And -- so you were working -- how long did you stay with Teddy Hill, was this just a week --
Something like a week, that's all. Apollo Theater, I couldn't make it.
I see.
Well, it didn't make sense to me, it was just a lot of hard work.
Yeah. Of course was Teddy Hill by himself -- went back to the days of Bessie Smith.
Yes. He did.
But then, on the other hand, he also was instrumental in the bop movement, he was running --
That's true, yes.
-- Minton's Playhouse.
That's right, yes.
So he had obviously made a transition in thinking then, he's musical thing --
He did, he did, yes.
And -- then you went with Eddie Heywood. Now this is the Eddie Heywood sextet, in '43, that was Eddie Heywood, Jr., right?
Yes.
And you had played with his father?
Yes.
Now that seem to have been a long lasting job?
It was.
You were there till '45?
Yes, that was a long lasting job.
And was this in New York or was this
traveling around.
All New York.
All in New York?
We didn't go anywhere with that band.
Stayed down at Cafe Society.
Now had you married at this point, yet?
Yes, I first married when I was with Alabamians, Hardy's Alabamians, then that's when I got -- when I first married.
I see and that -- so that was in the early '30's.
St. Paul, Minnesota.
Yes.
St. Paul, Minnesota.
In St. Paul?
Uh-huh.
And when was that -- in the '30's, early '30's?
Early '30's, yes.
Yeah.
Well that lasted seven years.
Uh-huh. So that when you went on vacation to Paris, in '39, you were no longer married?
That's right. Now wait a minute, '30, to
'37, I was married, then I was -- I married a second time and when I went on the vacation to Paris, I was married the second time, but it was on the rocks, also.
I see.

Because I could never buckle down to being married. You know, because it's very difficult for a musician -- during that time and even now, to settle down to married life. That's when you're going here and going there. It's very hard because you can't -- you don't have time for home life.
Right.

I mean I couldn't -- now some musicians could do that, but I didn't have time to settle down and say well I'm a married man, I've got to be home right after -- I got to do this, I got to do that, I could never buckle down to that.
You need a very understanding wife, I guess.
Yes, and I don't think there were very many around during that time.
Now you started teaching, you had your own studio here in New York?
Yes.
This was in the '40's?
'40's, yes.
When, about when was this?
This was after I left Cab's band.
Uh-huh.

I went to Nashville, I stayed -- I was down there in the hospital for about nine -- 10 days, you know, observation I had -- my sister was the superintendent of nurses at the Herbert Hospital in Mahari and naturally she always was interested in me, so she put me in the hospital, I stayed there nine days for observation, you know, chest and all that stuff, which I did have a problem with my chest, which wasn't serious as I thought it was at that time. So I didn't -- the doctors advised me not to -- told me to take a good rest, forget about playing for awhile. So I did, I didn't play for almost two years. So I came back to New York and I -- after I was down there for a while and I worked in the Post Office I was in the Post Office, GPO, went out to the was a postal concentration center for a long time.
And that's when I had a little studio also. I was teaching trumpet at the same time.
Uh-huh. And whom did you teach?

Well, I had quite a lot of kids down there. I don't think I had anybody that you know of. Because at that time the kids that I had about 40 -- 50 students. And they dwindled down to one, but in the meantime I had a little job at the Martinique, with the Marcelino Guerra.
Yes, you got into a whole latin thing.
Yeah.
AT one time and I want to -- want to get into that in a minute.
And I also did some recording, Bucking 2nd Bubbles, you know about that?
Well of course, I didn't know that you were -- what did you do with Bucking 2nd Bubbles?
Well, called me from the studio one day and said, they were recording and they said -- they sent for me to come up to the recording studio and I think, Bill Solomon Gomo was up there.
The trumpet player?

Yeah, he was in that -- made that session. They were having some trouble with getting the trumpet player to play the introduction, Bud Johnson was the contractor for the band. And he wrote something that the trumpet players couldn't play. So they sent for me to come up there just to play the introduction. I think the tune was "Turn Back the Clock," so I went up there and I played the introduction and that was all. I could go on back to the studio.
That's allyou did, just play the introduction?
Yeah, because you know being a lead
man for so long, those things are very easy for me.
Uh-huh.
And it was very hard -- difficult for a jazz man to play something like that Bud had written. So I went up there and played the introduction and I came on back to the studio.
Now when you had your studio and you were teaching, this is now in the what -- the mid '40's?
Yes.
Now this is when bebop was really flowering?
That's right.
And you were teaching young people?
Uh-huh.
They were interested in jazz, I assume?
Yes.
Were they interested in bop?
Yes, oh that's what they were interested in. They came to me, because you know a lot -- I was being recommended.
Uh-huh.
And they would come to me -- they'd get their mother, father, somebody go down and buy them a horn and get them a Dizzy Gillespie book and they'd come up to my

studio and say I want to study, I want to learn to play trumpet and they'd show me this book. This kid said, look I want to play like Dizzy. I said I can't teach you to play like Dizzy Gillespie. The first thing you got to do is learn to play your horn, you got to learn to play the horn first. You got to learn everything about it. No, I don't want to learn -- they say I don't want to go through the scales and all that I want you to teach me to play like Dizzy. I say I can't. I don't think Dizzy could teach you to play like that.

I say, Dizzy's a fine trumpet player. And he's a schooled trumpet player. Before he started playing what he's playing now. So you've got to go through all that and it's going to take years. And some of them I'd never see again. I'd run into that all the time. How long will it take me to learn to play the trumpet. I'd say, you may never learn to play trumpet. Only thing you can do is start or try, go through -- like the things that we all had to do, start from the bottom. Then you see what happens. I lost most of my pupils over latin trumpet players.

Yes, well I want to get into the latin thing, but before we get into that, I'd like to go back and -- over what we have just talked about, last hour and a half or so, and see did we leave anything out, were there any interesting things that happened, back in those early days, say leading up to 1945? Any experiences that you --

There's was a little job I had up in New London, Connecticut, with Tiny -- Tiny whatever his name is, little job didn't mean anything, it was just doing -- during the war and submarines were being built up in New London.
Tiny, who, Bradshaw?
