No. This a bass player, he used to work around New York. I can't remember his name right now, it'll come to me.
Uh-huh.

He had a little job at a beer joint up there and Wayman Carver was playing flute and saxophone, Gary Lee on drums, and Tiny was a bass player. We had a little job over there -- short, short job didn't last too long. That's about the only thing of interest that happened. It was just a short thing, that was before I joined Eddie Heywood.
What about -- were there -- did you have any incidents, like back in the Chicago days, what about the gangsters, they were very --
Oh yes, you see during that time all of the Cafes were supported by gangsters.
Right.
That was one of the only times we made any money at the Dreamland was when the gangsters came in here. And they would spend money, that was the only times they
would make any money.
They would tip you, right?
Oh, yes. Lord, they were very generous with their tips.
What was very generous?

Well they would come in and like take over the night, they'd close the doors, and nobody was there anyway, so that was their night. They'd take the night they would -- sometimes you'd come out a couple $100 in the kitty.
Now when you were at the Dreamland, I meant to ask you, were there any singers with the band at the Dreamland?
Well, we had a fellow by the name of George Dewey Washington. Who was very popular and Walter Richardson.
Uh-huh.

George Dewey Washington, and Walter Richardson, would sing at the Dreamland, like he would have them come in on weekends and sing. And they were very, very famous singers in Chicago at that time. They also sang at the Vendome.
And when you performed as accompanying singers, the singers got the tips, didn't they?
No, those tips were all divided equally.
Among the band and the singers.

I see, cause Lil Armstrong used to tell me about when she was accompanying Alberta in those clubs, Alberta would go from table to table and pick up the tips and she was supposed, to of course, share them with the accompaniest, but Lil suspected that she didn't always get her share.
No, I imagine she didn't. Lot of them they would holdout, sure, cause there'd be a lot of money.
Uh-huh.

Well, the singers like that they thought they were working harder than the band, but actually the band was working just as hard because they stay out on the floor sometimes an hour or over an hour. Sure, there was an act called Brown and McGraw, jazz dancers.
Uh-huh.

That Louis Armstrong made these -- this couple famous, cause he played every step they made. And he screamed the whole act, playing trumpet, and every movement that they made, Louis would make it on his horn, and that made Brown and McGraw one of the most famous dance acts in Chicago, at that time. And Brown and McGraw, when they would travel, they would look for some trumpet player to play because without a trumpet player their act didn't mean a thing. And so they had to have a good adlib jazz trumpet player to play to their act, like Jabbo Smith or that type of trumpet
player who could play their act or else the act was lost.

How do you feel when you see Hollywood movies that depict that era, say, well not talking about "Lady Sings the Blues," necessarily, did you see the television show with Ben Vereen playing Louis Armstrong?
I didn't see that. But I heard so much about it.
Uh-huh.
That -- but that it wasn't done properly, so much of it was --
No, it was pretty awful. But you've seen movies --
Oh, yes.
-- about the gangsters and the clubs and --
Oh yes. Oh, they don't tell the true story all the time.
No, they don't.
They leave most of the important things out of those films.
I mean the gangsters, did they look like those people we see in the movies?
I think so.
They did?
Yeah, they were very fine dressers,

but nice, friendly, but you could tell they were the boss, you know, a lot of them came in the Cotton Club, when I was with Cab, I knew a lot of them, they came over. We went to Sing Sing and played a little benefit, a whole Cotton Club show for one of the mobsters up there, he was in there.
Really, when was that?
That was during the time I was with Cab, at the Cotton Club.
You went to Sing Sing to play specifically for this one mobster?
That's right. That's right.
Who hired you for that?
Well, you see, I'm going to tell you something, you know, the Cotton Club was I think the -- as far as I know, most all of the Cotton Club was run by the mobsters, I think, that's what I heard.
They had to have some connection at Sing Sing in order to arrange that.

Yes, cause I remember I used to drink a little beer at the time, beer we used to drink up there, I forget the name of that beer, but they said it was all mobster controlled. The beer -- all the beer at the Cotton Club, and I'm quite sure they had a lot to do with the Cotton Club.
Uh-huh.
I'm quite sure they did. Because that
was money, I knew they would come in, they would come in there on weekends and they would take over.
You remember what year that was you played at Sing Sing?

Well that was during Cab's heyday, it was in the '30's. I don't exactly remember the year. It was either '30, before we did the "Big Broadcast." Cause we would go right from the Cotton Club in a bus, meet there and go right straight to Sing Sing and did this whole show, and all the girls the whole entire show, we played Sing Sing, for one of the fellows was up there serving time.
What about, getting back to Chicago, there were a lot of white musicians around in those days. Did you play with white musicians, did they come to the Clubs or what --
They would come to the clubs every night.
Uh-huh.
But we never had an opportunity to play with them. Sometimes they would maybe one would sit in.
Uh-huh.
With the band. Once in a very, very rare time, most of them would come and hear.
I see. Did you ever meet people like Bix Biederbeck?
I met Bix, yes. I met Benny Goodman.
Uh-huh.
I loved Jimmy Noon; I loved to hear him, I was up there most all the time, that's where I met Bix and Benny Goodman.
Of course Benny Goodman listened to Jimmy Noon a lot.
Oh, yes. He idolized him.
Now what did you -- do you remember what you thought of some of Bix's playing for instance?
It was an entirely new thing, I thought it was very exciting and very beautiful. I liked what Bix was doing.
Uh-huh.
Entirely different and I thought it was as nice to listen to as Louis Armstrong, also was different.
Well Rex Stewart was very taken by Bix, apparently.
He certainly was, yes. Yes.
And what about the Paul Whiteman band, for instance, did you like that kind of music?
I didn't like Paul Whiteman's band. Only time I enjoyed Paul Whiteman was when Bix was in the band. The only time. It was a good band. It was a good band, but
it didn't move me too much. Very well played band, I have to say that.
Yeah. Was it -- did you like playing in a big band -- I know you wanted to be with Cotton Pickers.
I've always wanted to play with big bands. I still want to play with a big band with strength, I've always wanted to do that --
Uh-huh.
-- never had the opportunity. I'd like to record with strings.

That was when -- when a lot -- when Charlie Parker recorded with strings and there was a period there where a lot -- Howard McGhee and a lot of people, Charlie Shavers, started making records with strings --
Uh-huh.
-- quite a few of the critics and the so-called purists, you know, looked on that as being so much commercial nonsense.
Yes, they did.
And I've always felt that most musicians liked pretty music.
Why certainly.
And really want to do this.
Yes, there's so much inspiration that we would get -- or we get, playing with strings.
Uh-huh.
Because you know it gives you an opportunity to express the harmony that you know, where you wouldn't get it -- be able to play it in every other type of band. When you work with strings.
Yes.
You take Clifford Brown and that guy's just out of sight with those strings that he recorded. I think -- you can appreciate them better with the strings than playing with this with a small group.
Uh-huh.
I think that strings bring out the beauty of a man's playing.

Now, what about people like Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith? Some musicians I have spoken to who were around that time but who were more sophisticated, shall we say, the New York musicians, tended to look down on those Southern blues people, they were a little bit too primitive for them, a little bit, not only in their music, but in their ways.
That's right.
Did you ever --
Oh, yes, that's true. We didn't appreciate so much playing with blues singers.
Uh-huh.

Not until -- I -- not until Joe Smith, when he came throughout the circuit with Ethel Waters, or Bessie Smith, one of those -- I have to go back to that, then that's when he played with a plunger, you know?
Uh-huh.
He did all his work with a plunger, behind this blues singer. Then the musicians started waking up to see how -- how it was a pleasure to play with the blues singers. That was done by Joe Smith.
I see.
He made it interesting to the musicians to play with them.

Because I know, Sam Wooding, for instance, very often when I speak to him, you know, he tends to make a little fun of Bessie Smith, he says, he recalls her coming up to Small's and singing and he said he could -- he could go to the bathroom, by the time he got out of the bathroom, she was just finishing the first line of her song. He always said to him, the blues singers seemed so very, very slow, they dragged everything out. That seems to have bothered Sam.
Well that's true, because you know the blues singers, at that time, they weren't appreciated.
Uh-huh.
I can -- I saw that in Nashville, be-

cause when the blues singers like Bessie or Clara Smith or Alberta Hunter Arnolds only same type of people would come to hear them. You would find the so-called elite, they would never come to the theater to hear Bessie Smith or any blues singer.
Uh-huh.
Ma Rainey would draw the roughest crowd -- element that you could find in Nashville and all out through the circuit.
Uh-huh.
(They wanted to come down there and hear (Unintelligible))

drunks and everybody else, but the so-called high class type of people, they didn't care for blues singing, blues singers. It was a long time before blues singers, you know, got really popular, people started getting interested in them, you know?
Uh-huh. How important was say, the Chicago Defender to -- to you when -- back in the '20's, and '30's, was that something you looked forward every week to read?
Oh, yes.
Defender and --
Oh, absolutely, yes.
-- to find out what was happening in the business,
That's right. Yes. We thought that was a great paper.
Because the black show business world
was quite separate from the white.
Oh, absolutely, yes. Yes. Chicago Defender really gave you all the news of the entertainment in Chicago at that time.
Right, and the white papers weren't bothering with that.
-- bothered at all, didn't mean a thing.
And you also, people used to get their mail --
Oh, surely.
-- right through -- at the Chicago Defender?
Absolutely, yes.
But did you read, for instance, white papers?
Well, no, I didn't really didn't. I only read the Chicago Defender.
Uh-huh. And I guess the Amsterdam Newsly Run.
Amsterdam News, the Afro-American.
Do you remember the Interstate Tattler?
Oh, yes.
That was a little gossip sheet, wasn't it?
Gossip sheet, yes. Yes.
And there was a man, let's see what was his name, who -- who ran that paper?
No, no, I don't remember. Right now.
I heard that he was very famous because if you saw him, you sort of made sure you were behaving when he was around, because --
Yes.
-- otherwise it would get in --
I should know who that was, I just tell you -- right now I can't -- you took me back that time, yes. I remember very well, Tattler.
Yeah. Did you ever travel with tent shows?
I did two days with a tent show from Nashville. I'd runup for the summer. I did two days with a tent show, I couldn't make it.
No? What was the show do you remember?
Well, it was like they had a comedians and dancers and chorus girls, and we'd have to play outside the tent show, about a half an hour to attract the people from the grounds.
Uh-huh.
So we did a show out there, a short show to bring the people inside. We were blowing continuously. Then, we'd go inside and then the people would come in and we'd

do show and then we'd go right back out, do the same thing over and over again and my lip just split right down the middle, and I couldn't take it, I had to give up after two -- you were playing all day.
Uh-huh. You don't remember whose tent show that was?
I don't remember.
When was that?
Oh, gosh, that was before -- that was real early, that was in the early '20's, I'd say maybe around '20, '24, something like that.
When you were still living in --
Nashville.
Nashville.
I did that for about two days, I left, I couldn't make it.
Uh-huh.

I played circuses too. Circuses come through Nashville, we had a band there, fellows much older than I. But we would play, like Ringling Brothers would come to Nashville, they would hire us to play for the parade, anyway.
Nashville is now the capital of country music --
Yes, it is.
-- but there must've been a lot of
country music around then.
There was country music, there, sure. Country music. My father played mandolin, he was -- he played that type of stuff. I heard a lot of that in Nashville.
So there were blacks playing country music?

I don't know of any blacks playing, I know my father was a mandolin player, but I don't know I never heard his being connected with any group like that but most of the country musicians that I heard were all white.
Uh-huh.
Turkey in the Straw type of musicians, you know?
Yeah. How do you like that music?
Well, I like it, I'm not going to say anything against it, I'm from Nashville, you know, I'm not going to saying anything against country music. In fact I was there last week.
You still have family in Nashville.
I have a brother, retired brother there.
Uh-huh.
Dentist, he's retired there.
You're not related to Jimmy Cheatham are you?
We're sort of distant related, yeah.
You are. Now I made a mistake in my book on Bessie, apparently, I mentioned you in there, somebody told me they had spoken to you that it wasn't you, it was another Cheatham, I think, in Detroit --
You mean Ohio, that was Richard, Dick Cheatham.
Dick Cheatham?
Yeah, Richard.
Uh-huh.
He was a famous -- he was a pianist. He's the one that had that band.
And he was not related to you?
No, not at all.
[PAUSE]
I see. All right, well let's get into this Latin music. How did you ever -- did your experience in Barcelona have anything to do with you getting into Latin music?
Oh, no. Barcelona was there, we were just doing our regular thing. You know.
You heard a tango band there?

I heard, I liked tango music, because I thought [Canaro] had -- course for the first time hearing a tango band I thought it was very beautiful music, but I never thought -- it never influenced me one way or the other.
Uh-huh.

But, the band I worked with here, was Marcelino Guerrero, I was just going up as a substitute, you know, and I didn't care too much about it at all. Because the band was a great band, but it didn't -- move me.
This was in the '40's, in what, '46, '7?
It was around '45, around that time.
It was around the time when Dizzy started doing a lot of things?
Yes, yes. Around '45, early '46.
Uh-huh.

And I worked Martinique, as a substitute with the band. They liked me and I found it interesting, of course everything was reading and it was a a -- challenge. Quite different from reading American scores. So I stayed with them quite awhile. They broke up and then I went with Machito.
Uh-huh.

I worked with Machito for awhile -- they fired me out of that band because I couldn't understand it. I couldn't understand the beat. I couldn't understand it at all. But they hired me back later -- I made up my mind I said, I'm going to see what this is all about. Buckle down and play with a lot of small Latin groups until I learn how
to play with the beat, because you just can't jump in there and play that music.
Yeah.
And I stayed with Machito -- went to Japan with Machito. I stayed with him, recorded with him quite a long time after that. And I liked it but I still wanted to play jazz but there wasn't any work.
Oh, so you went into Latin music because of lack of work --
Uh-huh.
-- in jazz, not because you had a particular fondness for Latin music?

I like it. When I was with Benny Goodman, same thing happened, I came back and I was playing at -- I was a substitute with Ricardo Rey, that was one of the greatest little Latin bands that I ever heard. It was more of a jazz than it was Latin. They'd just begin to integrate, you know, that music.
Uh-huh.
Making it -- like Tito Puente's doing, bringing American jazz in with the Latin rhythms. I stayed with Ricardo Rey, four years.
Now you were also with Claude Hopkins. Where does that fall in? Does that --
I only worked with Claude Hopkins in
Atlantic City and early, early '20's at the -- place called the Bellman's Inn. I used to play with him down there.
In the early '20's?

Yes. 'That was like I'll go through Nashville, go out there for the summertime, sametime that I was in Nashville, I worked with Charlie Johnson. The same time. I was fired from Charlie Johnson's band, and so I was pushing chairs on the boardwalk and I also would go down and play with Claude Hopkins, but I wasn't a member of the band. I was never a member of Claude Hopkins' band.
Oh, because this book, here, says you were with Hopkins in 1946.
Uh-uh.
But that's not so, not true. John Chilton got his information wrong.
I've done some -- quite a few jobs with Claude Hopkins.
But you didn't mention the Charlie Johnson band before, now that was a great band, wasn't it?
Oh, yes.
And that was at the Paradise, wasn't it?
In Atlantic City. They would work in Atlantic City in the summer and the winter they would come here, to Small's Paradise.
Right.
They did that every year.
And let's see, what year was it that you were with Johnson?
That was around '24, '25.
Uh-huh.
Was Frankie Half-Pint Jackson there then?
That's right, that's right.
What was he like, he was very small, right?
Very small, very neat, immaculate fellow.
Uh-huh.

And he could put a song over like you know, nobody in the world could. I'll never forget him. In fact, I do one of his songs now. I started a little singing thing, I do one of his songs now. Every now and then, he was just great. Fact, all the entertainers in those days were great.
Now he was a singer and he also led a band for awhile?
Yes, he was a little band leader, liked to jump up and direct.
Was he sort of a musical director at the Paradise in Atlantic City?
Well I don't think he was the musical director, he was more of an entertainer.
Uh-huh.

But you know Charlie Johnson had a habit of getting up from his piano, and going out maybe somewhere, leave the band playing without a piano and he was the first one to do that and the band played very well without him. He'll do that all the time. Get up and leave the band. He'd go home, or go out and sit down, listen to his band. His band played very well without him. And maybe a guy like Half-Pint, he used to jump up there in front of the band, and clown and direct the band, that's about all.
Uh-huh. What would you say was the -- back then, in your early days in the '20's. What were the great events in your life?
Like what? Now let's see.
In your career, what did you want to be in those days? Did you want to be another Louis Armstrong, or did you --
Well, after hearing Louis Armstrong, and Freddie Keppard Gebhardt, and then I heard -- I was impressed also by a fellow named Bob Shafner Staffner --
Who replaced Louis with King Oliver,
right? I knew I would never be another Louis Armstrong, I had no even thought about that.
Uh-huh.

But I wanted to be able to play like him. I wanted to be able to understand how he played and why he played certain things at different times. In fact I was on his tail all the time, studying little cliches that he would do. Course, naturally, a lot of them he learned from King Oliver. Course, I also listened to King Oliver a long time.
Yes, now how did you like King Oliver?

I liked King Oliver, but he never played too much when I would go to listen to him. Cause it was mostly an ensemble band, but he played like short solos. I thought he was a very, very fine. And I could hear Joe Oliver's playing, (unintelligible) in Louis Armstrong's playing until he died. I could hear little things. They were little cliches that they would have among themselves. Red Allen has it too.
Yes.
Little things that probably nobody else would pay attention to.
What about Louis's singing?
Well, I thought it was sensational. It was sensational, right from the beginning. I don't think anybody found anything wrong with it.
Well, he was such a showman, very outgoing.
Oh, yes, he was a showman, in fact anything Louis Armstrong did was a sensation.
Uh-huh.

Anything he did. Even on the streets, he would walk up the street, laughing and joking, his belly shaking fat, you know, and he was just a funny, jolly fellow all the way around. Everything he said was funny.
Uh-huh.

Joking, wonderful jokes, you know. He was just an ordinary -- extraordinary man. And I don't think anybody ever will be able to play like him. I didn't have any idea of ever playing like him, but I wanted to get in there and see what was inside of it, you know. Not only Louis, but you could hear lot of this same things among, with Joe Oliver, Red Allen, Bob Scheffner, they all had something in common.
Well I was wondering because you inherited that band all of a sudden, you found yourself being a band leader at the Dreamland, and you really -- you -- most of your career, you've been a side man --
All the time, yes.
And I just wondered whether you didn't have ambitions to start then -- why you didn't start

Well, I never thought of it. I remember when I left Cab, Cab asked me -- he said would you like me to book you? I didn't know what he was talking about, he said I would like to -- would you like for me to book you as a band, or something like that and I said no. I didn't want that. I wasn't interested in that. Band leaders and side men are too different things. I wanted to be a trumpet player, not a band leader, cause you go in as band leader, then something's missing. Something is taken away from you. You've got to worry about individuals.
You have all that responsibility.
You've got all that responsibility and I think all that takes from your playing.
But, on the other hand it was a better way to make money, being a band leader, right?
That's true, but I didn't want to make money, that wasn't what I wanted, I didn't care about money. I only wanted to play.
You just wanted to live comfortably?
I didn't care anything about money.
Uh-huh.
I wanted to play. I wanted to play, that was the only thing. And I was confused. Cause then I'd hear Charlie Shavers, I wanted to throw my horn away. I said

I'd hear what is this? Damn, Roy at the Three Deuces, what the hell is this, then I'd come and I'd hear Jabbo. I'd hear Cuban Cube, man, I didn't know what to do, I said, damn, that was my problem. I wanted to play. Money didn't mean anything to me. That's why I worked for Sam Wooding for $75.00 to Europe. I wasn't worried about money, because I was sitting beside Tommy Ladner, side-talking to Ladner.
Where did you hear Jabbo Smith?
In New York.
In New York. Who was he with then?
Well, I only heard him, like, at jam sessions. I never heard him play with any bands.
In the '20's, did you listen -- there wasn't too much jazz on the radio, but did you listen to a lot of records?
Yes, oh, yes. Oh yes. The first recording that I heard was Johnny Dunn. A trumpet player.
Johnny Dunn, sure.
Now he was exciting.

Now he was apparently very popular, because I have a ledger right here, it's from the early days of Columbia in the '20's, and it shows all the recordings that were made and how much they were paid and I notice that Johnny Dunn got paid more than most people, most recording artists.
I wouldn't be surprised.
So he must've been --
Yes, he had about the first hit record. Of any trumpet player, I think.
And what was that?
"Bugle Call Rag."
Oh, his "Bugle Call Rag," of course.
That was a hit record all over -- even -- when a record would get to Nashville, you know it had to be a hit. All over the world that record was sold.
Did you ever meet him?
Yes. I met him with the show in Atlantic City, he was in the show. One of those shows. I attended all those shows, you either Shuffle Along or Dixie Broadway, one of those shows, he was in the pit.
Uh-huh.
I also met him in Baltimore somewhere. He was from around that area.
Yeah.
He was sensational.
So, when you heard somebody like Johnny Dunn on a record, and I assume you were listening to "Bugle Call Rag," for instance, did you then try to play along with the record?
I played it, yes I did. I learned it exactly like he did. Uh-huh. I played it all over Nash-
ville, at little dances I played it. I played the "Bugle Call Rag" just like Johnny Dunn.
Uh-huh.
Wrote it down, I mean I didn't write it, played it, copied it in my mind. I did that all the time.
So records were important to --
Very important.
-- musicians like yourself?
Oh yes. Cause we didn't get a chance to hear too many -- Johnny Dunn, Fate Marble, and Charlie Creath was the only three trumpet players that I heard in Nashville, during the time I was in Nashville.
In person, you mean?
Well some of them recordings, some of them in person.
Uh-huh.
They would never come to Nashville, but I heard them like from recordings.
I see, but you weren't really listening to any of the white ones, the white players?

No, because I didn't hear anyone that I liked, at that time. There was a guy called Louie Panico, I thought he was -- he did a little something with a wa-wa mute, I liked that, but it proved to be nothing after listening to some jazz, man, what he was doing was nothing.
But, at that time, I was -- to hear a trumpet make cat calls, all over the wa-wa mute, it excited everybody.
Now, you did hear Freddy Kephard?
Oh yes.
In person?
Yes.

Now they've always said about Freddy Kephard that he was so afraid people would -- other trumpet players would copy him and there's an old story that he used to play with a handkerchief over his valves so that --
That's right, so you wouldn't see what he was fingering.
And that's a true story?

That's a true story. One day in Chicago, the word got out that Freddy Kephard played -- was playing and he blew a note so loud that he -- that the straight mute that he was playing jumped clean out of his horn, went all away across the night club floor. He hit this note, and so naturally everybody went up there, all the musicians would go up to hear Freddy Kephard, to see him do it again. But he never did it again.
Did you ever talk to anyone who was there a -- that night?
Well, no, I only heard the rumor, it was a lot of musicians, everything that happend in Chicago

those days, you would hear it through the musicians. Everything that Louis did or anybody else did, you would hear from the musicians and naturally you go round to see who's doing it. What was happening. Yeah, that was the way Freddy was, he didn't want anybody to steal his ideas, so naturally he's covered up his fingering.
How did he compare to some of the others?

Well, you couldn't compare him with Louis Armstrong. I don't think he had the taste that Louis Armstrong had. (or Sheffner or Bob Sinnes) Red Allen. He wasn't as tasty as -- he was real crude, you know. But good.
But good.
And you had to hear him because he was very loud.
He was loud?
Very loud. But he wasn't as tasty as the rest of the guys.

Now what about some of the -- well let's say, the -- when the bands came in and the bands were playing arrangements. I know Elmer Snowden told me many times that very often, when he had a band, they would remove the name of the tune from the music sheets --
Yes, that's true.
-- so that others couldn't --
Tell what they'er playing, that's right.
And Elmer, in fact, also used to -- the strings on his banjo were reversed in some ways, so if anyone else picked up his banjo, --
They couldn't play it.
-- they couldn't play it.
That's right.
Why was all that -- you know --
Well, you know, the musicians -- some of them in those days, they wanted to be -- they had a feeling that you were going to steal something from them. Or take something from them.
Uh-huh.
Or learn something from them. They didn't want you to do that. I know a trumpet player here in New York that used to turn his back to the audience. And play.
Before Miles Davis did?
Yes, way before Miles. He would get up and play his solo and turn his back to the audience.
Who was that?
Fellow named Hatton.
Hm.
Now this was a guy, the first guy that every used -- that I ever know of -- that used a mute, he started

these things about these buckets, hats and bottles, before they ever made a mute, he was using bottles and tin buckets, shoes and everything in his horn. That was way before they started making mutes. Named Jack Hatton.
But, musicians were making records all this time and certainly, there's nothing easier than copying off a record, you did that yourself?
I did it myself. That's true, you could -- you couldn't keep a guy from copying --
Right.
-- but I don't know you could -- they would make little things that would hide the valves, so you wouldn't see what they were playing. If they recorded them, you couldn't stop them from copying.
They just did everything to make it difficult.
They wanted to --
Did you ever worry about someone taking your ideas?

No, no I didn't because I didn't think I had any ideas, I was too busy trying to learn, I didn't worry about those things. I never felt myself that good. You know I wanted to -- I was, as I said, confused. Very confused. I didn't know what I wanted to do. And being a saxophone player too, had a lot to do with my trumpet playing.
Yeah, how so?
Well, because I was playing a lot of jazz saxophone and when you -- also and playing trumpet switching to trumpet you find yourself playing the same thing that you've playing on the saxophone.
Uh-huh.

Arpeggios the same arpeggios. I had to get all of that out of my system. And I was too busy learn- ing, I didn't worry about anyone listening to me, at that time. I was too busy. Bobby Hackett came on the scene, that was another problem. He worked with Cab one night.
Oh, he did?
Yes.
When you were with Cab?

Yes, we were up at Sunland (somewhere in New England) during that time, and I think one of our trumpet players was sick or something, Bobby came in and played. I never heard of Bobby Hackett. And he upset everybody. So I started buying his records. And going on like that. I never worried about anything like that. I was too busy, and I'm still the same way today. I hear too many things I'd like to do.

Well, Lil Armstrong told me that she used to -- she would -- it was a long time before she realized that -- oh before any of them realized that the music they were playing was of any importance, that was going to be
That's true.
And it was just a matter of making money and doing it.
That's all, yes.
When did you first realize that jazz music was -- it was going to be taken seriously?
Well, I would say that in 1967.
As late as 1967?
How was that?
Because I'd say, as I said before, I had no feeling of ever being well known as a trumpet player.
Uh-huh.

I never had that feeling. I was just trying to push myself to learn so much and then, after 1967, I was beginning to get calls from people, asking questions, writing books and invited here to play this jazz thing, go to Europe. I went to Europe, I guess it was George Wein and (unintelligible). I had recorded with George Wein, which I didn't think amounted to anything, I never thought that I would --
Oh, so it was in 1967 you realized that --
I realized --
-- of your importance?
Yes, that's right.
But when did you realize the importance of the music you represented, you know, of jazz?
That's right, the same time, the same time.
But when you were in Europe, and you recorded for Charles Delauney --
With Sam?
No, I mean later when you recorded for Charles Delauney --
Well, you know what I was thinking of that time -- because at that time when I was in Europe, there was no other trumpet player there. I was the only one there.
Oh, you thought it was --

Now being fresh from New York, from America, they pick on you. You fresh from New York, they don't care they pick on you right away, Oh, he's just from New York, from America, so we're going to record him. That's the only time I ever recorded for Charles Delauney.
Uh-huh.
I never knew him before.
But when did you first become aware of the fact that there were writers writing about jazz, books out on the subject and so forth? You must've become aware of that in the '30's, didn't you?

I did because that -- was one book I have, I think I have the book where there was -- an Esquire jazz book I think in the '30's, where they said Doc Cheatham the greatest first trumpet player in the world, and I didn't like that. Cause I didn't want to be called a first trumpet player. Benny Carter had a write-up somewhere, recently, a few years ago, that he said Doc Cheatham's the greatest first trumpet -- was, at that time, greatest trumpet player in the world. And I didn't like that I didn't want to be branded as a lead trumpet player and that is the thing that hurt me for so many years, because I wanted to play jazz. But I jumped into the lead trumpet playing because no one wanted to play lead trumpet.

I joined Chick Webb's band, I went there that night, there was Freddie Jenkins, I don't know what other trumpet player but they all sat down and left the first trumpet chair open and nobody seated there. And the book, so naturally I went and sat, and played the lead.
Uh-huh.

And that happened for years, nobody wanted to play first, because there were no solos in the first -- on the first book. So I did it and I liked it and I said I may as well try to be a first trumpet player.
Uh-huh. Did you ever want to play with Duke Ellington's band?
I had an offer to play with Duke, just before he died.
Oh, this was recently.
Before he went to Tokyo, yes.
But back in the, because Duke's band --
Oh, yes.
-- been around so long.

Oh, yes. I wanted so bad to play with Duke's band. I wanted very much to play with Duke. I thought I had an opportunity, at one time, Juan Tizol came over to the Cotton Club and took me to see Duke, says, I think Duke can use you. So he took me over there to the theater, where Duke was playing. And I went -- he took me in the dressing room and set me down there. Duke and I had a talk, he was making up and going on the stage, I sat there for an hour boy he didn't say anything to me about working with his band. I sat there for one hour and I stayed the whole, till they got through. He didn't say one thing about offering me a job. So, I've always wanted to work with Duke, that's my type of band.
He did -- I did get an offer from him just before he went to Tokyo, the last time, but I didn't accept it because I -- I was doing a little better than what he offered at that time.
Uh-huh.
And I didn't want jump on the band -- I didn't know what I'd have to do there. I didn't want to jump in a band playing lead. I don't do -- I can't do that anymore. That's out.
When did your family finally accept you as a jazz musician?
Well --
Or did they ever?

-- as soon as they found out -- learned that I was taking care of myself. That was their main worry. They knew I was taking care of myself and I was keeping in touch with them all the time. I'd go to see them all the time. Send money every week to my mother, send things to my father. Clothes, and things --
Uh-huh.

-- and they knew where I was all the time, then they began to -- they knew that everything was all right. They knew they couldn't stop me, because that was what I had to do. So they knew that I was taking good care of myself. They knew where I was all the time, every day practically they knew where I was.
So they accepted it?
They accepted it, they began to feel little proud -- we played Nashville with Cab's band and my mother came to see the concert we played there and
they felt very proud of me, of me then.
Well --

Because I didn't let them down, I didn't become a drunk -- they was afraid of that. You know they worried about your not living -- taking care of yourself, eating right, you know how parents were in those days?
Yeah.
But they accepted it because I didn't -- they didn't have to worry about me at all.

I want to -- in our next session I want to get into -- go from say mid-'40's up to the present time. But, just before we stop this, let me just see if there's anything else we have left out. What would you say up to 1946, what -- what was the high light -- the high point of your career, was it Cab Calloway band, was it the Cotton Pickers?
It was the Cab Calloway band.
The Cab Calloway band.
Cab's a very important part of my life.
Now that was a lot of travelling, it was very popular band --
Lot of travelling, but first class.
Uh-huh, but you didn't mind the touring?
I didn't mind it because it was all first class. We had no -- it wasn't like the Cotton Pickers, or the Alabamians where you were riding buses, a -- old raggedy buses, break down every few miles.
Uh-huh.
Sleeping in the buses, eating cold cuts, being run out of places, being run out of town and all this stuff. With Cab it was first class all the way. Slept on Pullmans' side track to sleep.
Uh-huh.
Eat the best we could.
Did you ever meet Blanche Calloway?
Sure, know Blanche very often.
Now, some people have told me that Blanche actually had a better band, at one time, that she was -- she ended up in a mental institution, didn't she?
Well, at present she's in -- she's in Miami, she's a disc jockey there.
Oh, is she really?
Uh-huh.
Did you ever hear her band when she had a band?
Yes. I don't think she had a better band than Cab. She had a good band, but I don't think it was any better than Cab. I think both those bands were equal.
But her band was better known at one point?
It was better known, well she was a better entertainer, at that time, before Cab became popular.
Uh-huh.
She was -- oh, she was a much better entertainer than Cab. See Cab came along with this gimmick, you know.
Yes, the hidey-hi.
That's what did it and then you heard (unintelligible) Blanche Calloway. But Blanche was a great entertainer.

What about Jim Crow in those days, with the Cab Calloway band. Now the band was very popular, it appeared in movies and, obviously, it was a band that attracted a lot of white people also, or was known among white people.
Yes.
And when you were touring, what -- were there incidents, was it --

Oh, were there incidents. We were in Memphis, Tennessee, and at the end of the dance, there was a white girl came up -- woman -- for Cab's autograph. And you know how Cab, reach over the stand, his hair would fall right on down. And the biggest fight started you ever saw in
your life.
Because his hair fell?
Because this woman came up and his hair fell down like that. I don't know why that -- I mean the fight started then.
Uh-huh.

Chairs, bottles, everything, the biggest fight you ever saw in your life in the ballroom. Free-for-all, throwing at the band, fighting the band. Chairs, I got behind a table. I just got behind a table. I can't fight. Then a pig got his knife out and it was a good fight. Cops came and hustled Cab out, took him out the back and put him in a car, and we didn't see Cab anymore until we got on the train. But they were fighting us all the way out of the ballroom, all the way from the -- in the automobiles, on the highways, till we got all the way to the train. Throwing bricks at the cars, everything, all the way till we got to the Pullman car. Cab was in the Pullman car, sleeping.
When was this, do you remember?
Actually, the year, I can't remember that, it in the '30's, the dates, I don't remember. I don't remember the date of that.
And there were many incidents similar?
There was not too many. We are -- were in Miami and first time the band was in Miami. We were

playing there at a big place there, it was a white place, did not allowed colored in it. So a couple of guys standing out in the front heckling the band, you know, and they -- one called me, and I went over there cause I was a Southerner and I don't have problems with the Southerners. This guy had a big glass of corn whiskey and say have a drink. I says, I don't drink. He says, you will drink this. So, I drank the whole glass of corn whiskey, and man I mean I was so drunk I didn't know where I was.

And at the end of that they just started throwing things. They threw a bottle up there and it hit the drummer in the head, knocked a hole in his head. That was in Miami, we had to be hustled out of there.
Uh-huh. What about the hotels, that must've been a problem...
Well, we couldn't stay at hotels, we just had to -- that's why we had the Pullman. We had a Pullman we kept all the time.
Cause you slept on the train?
Course, you slept on the train. So we weren't allowed to go anyplace to eat or anything, just had to find colored restaurants or eat -- have stuff brought to the car.
Didn't that make you bitter?
It didn't make me bitter, because I

was a Southerner, I was used to that. I'd been run out of places in Nashville, as a kid. After playing a beautiful job, like out to the Belle Meade Country Club, I was coming out one night after finishing a job and we were (unintelligible) bringing the instruments, and a white girl and her boyfriend, people coming home from -- she said mister, can I beat on your drum and I said, Lady, no, she said -- and the guy said, well if we can't beat on that drum, we're going to beat on your head, so I put the drums, and I said, well you help yourselves (to beat on the drums). You know. I'm used to that because the Southerners never bothered me. I just know, how they are. So, travelling through the South never bothered me. I didn't expect to go walk into a restaurant, sit down and eat.

One day Claude Jones did it, though. Claude Jones, he could actually pass. Claude Jones did it -- we were side-tracked into this -- right across, old beat grease joint, Claude Jones, went on in the restaurant, sat down at the counter and they served him. We didn't do it, but he could pass.

So, I think Lamar Wright (unintelligible) spied him, you know, in there and I think Lamar Wright (unintelligible) somebody went in there and sat down by him and said oh, if Claude could go in there, so -- I think it was Lamar, went in there sat down beside him and the man, said what the hell are you -- you know and then ran Claude and Lamar out of the joint.
Hm.
Because you know you run into those
things.
Right.
But it never bothered me and I expected it, you know. But it made -- it upset some guys, but it didn't bother me. I knew what to do and I knew what was expected and it didn't bother me.
Hm.

See, I'd get my food and I'd go somewhere and buy something or go in the back of the restaurant and the man give it to me and I'd walk on out the door take it on back and eat it, in the bus. But it didn't bother me. But it would bother, I guess musicians that born in the North, you know, places like that.
Right.
It didn't bother me at all, not one bit.
Because you grew up with this?
Yeah, I grew up with it and that mess down there.
Now, what I'm going to do first, is, instead of picking up where we left off, you know, I'm going to go back --
Uh-huh.
-- and I've dug up some names and I want to see if they --
Yeah, all right.
-- ring a bell with you.
Okay.

Now, a lot of the people I mention, things I mention, probably these are things that happened, people who were around before you came to Chicago, I believe, but they may still have been around when you were there --
Uh-huh.
-- and I just want to make sure. Now, Lawrence Duke Dewey, for instance.
Uh-huh.
Do you remember --
I remember that name. I just can't --

He was a clarinet player, had a band with Sugar Johnny, and well Sugar Johnny, you probably don't remember, he was a trumpet player -- but he died of tuberculosis and he was replaced by Freddy Kefford Kephart.
I see, no, I didn't know him at all.
And Jimmy P. 130 Palow, violinist?
No, I didn't know him.
Roy Palmer?
I remember Roy Palmer.
Fred Hall?
Fred Hall, I don't, what's he, bass player?
Yes.
Yes.
Do you remember, singer, named Dovey?
Dubbie?
Dovey.
Dovey, no.
No. Do you remember a place, a gambling joint called (the) Pioneer Club?
I remember that.
What was that like, was it strictly for black people?
Well, I guess so, you know, I didn't attend any of those types of clubs, I wasn't interested too much in those type of places, you know?
Uh-huh.
At that time, you know, I was so wrapped up in music, so much that I didn't attend any of those type of places.
But you knew --
I knew of it, yes.
Uh-huh.
Oh, yes.
What about Curtis Moseby?
I remember that name, too. Curtis Moseby, I remember him.
He had a band, apparently.
Yes, I remember him, vaguely. The name.
But you didn't know him?
No.
Now do you remember the Deluxe?
Yes. I remember the Deluxe.
And Izzy Shore?
No.
Izzy Shore -- from what I gather was the person who was proprietor of the Deluxe Cafe. Now it was called -- I think it was Deluxe Saloon and Billiards Club.
Uh-huh.
And there was this Cafe and a doorman name Jones, he used to stand outside.
Yeah, that's King Jones. That was King Jones.
King Jones?
Yes, they called him King Jones.
Uh-huh. And he used to be a sort of barker?
Yes. Well he went from club to club. As a barker, you know, he'd also announced the shows, attractions, the acts that would follow. He was just a loud-mouthed
guy, tried to talk with an English accent.
With an English accent?
Yeah, he tried to talk with an English accent.
And, now, I'm going to mention some entertainers who were at the Deluxe.
Uh-huh.
In the '20's.
Uh-huh.
And, let me just fix your microphone here. Now some entertainers at the Deluxe. Do you -- Florence Mills, of course.
Yes, I knew Florence Mills.
Yes, but do you remember Florence Mills being at the Deluxe?
Yes, I heard of her being at the Deluxe, although I didn't, you know, it was just another performer, I didn't -- she didn't become real famous, I don't think till she came to New York with the show.
'Shuffle Along.'
'Shuffle Along, yes. I knew of her, yes.
Now there were some girls who worked with her. Cora Green.
Yes. I knew Cora Green.
Can you tell me anything about these people, that I mentioned?

Well, you know, as I said before, they were very famous, I mean popular in Chicago and that was the time -- I had just arrived in Chicago at that time and so I didn't come in contact with them personally, but as a musician working in the clubs there, I did know of them.
Uh-huh.
Cora Green and Florence Mills, by name, but I didn't come in contact with any of them, at all.
What about Twinkle Davis?
I remember that name too. But -- the same thing, I didn't come in contact with them.
Mamie Maime Carter?
No, I didn't know Mamie Maime Carter.
Well, Mattie Hite?
Mattie Hite I knew very well.
Well what about -- tell me about her?
Well, I met Mattie Hite in Atlantic City, at the Bellman's Club, that's where Claude Hopkins had the group there.
Uh-huh.
Oh, she was a very good entertainer. She sang at all tables, you know, from table to table, that
was her style -- the style in those days.
Uh-huh.

And she would keep the band playing for maybe a couple of hours. Once -- during one song. And she had a lot of -- most of her songs were very risqué. And she'd pick up a lot of money, you know, going from table to table singing these risqué type of songs.
She had a high pitched voice?
Had a pitched -- high pitched type of voice, sort of --
Like Ollie Powers?
Yes. That's right, yes. Very good entertainer.
What about Goldie Crosby?
Goldie Crosby? I didn't know Goldie Crosby.
Nellie Carr?
No.
Did you know a pianist named George Hall?
I know George Hall, I remember him.
Was he a good pianist?
Well, I guess so. I guess he was a good pianist. He was all right. In those days there was only two great pianists in Chicago at that time and that was Teddy
Weatherford and Earl Hines.
Uh-huh.
So the rest of them, they were good, but they didn't get the recognition that Earl Hines and Teddy Weatherford got. As pianists.
I learned about George Hall from Lil Armstrong.
Uh-huh.
Who told me that he could teach her a few things.
Yes, I guess so. That was his way, you know?
Did you ever hear, I guess you didn't hear Bill Johnson's band at the Royal Garden?
No, I didn't hear Bill Johnson, although I did hear a band at the Royal Garden, I don't remember, I thought it had -- it was King Oliver's band --
Yes.
-- that was the band that I heard at the Royal Garden.
Right that was a little later.
Uh-huh.
Now you say the Dreamland, by the time you got to it, you went in there with Al Wynn Williams --
Yes.
Bill Bottoms had left --
Yes.
-- sort of become run down?
Yes.
But you did go to it while Bill Bottoms was running it?
Yes.
Didn't you?
Yes, I went there.
Do you remember his two floormen, Johnny Brown and Bill George?
No, I didn't know them.
Didn't know them?
Uh-uh.
What about some of the members of the Oliver band, the Dodds Brothers, Dutrey, did you know any of them?
I met a few of them, but you see, at that time, when I saw or heard Oliver's band at the Royal Garden, I wasn't playing there, I was just there on a vacation.
Uh-huh.

In the summertime. I had a relative living on the South Side and I would stay with them, and I wasn't playing, in fact, I didn't play at all in Chicago during that time. But I went around to the Royal Gardens and a few
Now you went to Dreamland in the Bill Bottom days. Who did you hear there? Did you hear Ollie Powers, Alberta Hunter?
Yes, Alberta Hunter, I heard her there. Ollie Powers was also -- yes.
Was Alberta, was she a big thing there?
She was a big thing then, at that time, yes. Alberta was a big star at the Dreamland.
She was fairly young, too?
Fairly young, yes. She was very nice, very fine entertainer. Singer, Alberta Hunter.
She introduced some new songs?
Yes, yes.
Do you remember what the shows were like, did the do a lot of talking or --
Well the shows were, you know, they had they had what you competition shows, you know, each club tried to have the best floor show.
Uh-huh.
And they had -- they had very spectacular shows, costumes and chorus girls and dancers and singers. And there was a -- I think a fellow named Norman
Thomas, he was the best of producers of shows, night club shows, in Chicago at that time. He had the most spectacular shows of any producer in Chicago, during that time.
And where did he produce shows?

He produced shows over on the Sunset and across the street from the Sunset, I forget the name of what they call it. Club. There were two clubs, one right across the street from the other. Sunset and -- what the heck is the name of that club, where Carroll Dickerson Cal-Dixon had a band there. Forget the name of that club, I could never remember. But he was the producer of those shows in those clubs.
Uh-huh.
I think he may have done some stuff, producing at the Grand Terrace, I'm not too sure, but he was the greatest of all producers, show producers.
Did you ever go to the Lorraine Gardens?
Oh, yes, I went to the Lorraine Gardens.
Now the Lorraine, from what I understand, was sort of a slightly lower class than Dreamland?
Oh, yes. Oh, yes, it was, sort of lower class during that time. That was when the Dreamland was very popular, it was lower class type of a place.
Now, what kind of people came into

Well the Dreamland was -- it was on State Street, kind of out of the way from the other clubs. And they had quite a lot of kind of people from downtown. Came to the Dreamland. Mostly lot -- in other words, it was like the Congress Inn, here, compared with that. And quite a lot of pimps and gangsters.
And what -- now this is during the Prohibition, of course, and what -- they didn't serve lemonade, did they?
No. Well they just served whiskey, bootleg whiskey. And beer, bootleg beer.
Uh-huh. So that subjected them to raids, I would imagine?
Oh, yes. They were often raided, raided every now and then, yes.
And was the liquor served openly?
No, not openly, no. You know you could get it, the waiter would bring it in like a pint, something like that a quart. I f you pay for it, but they wasn't serving it openly, no. But it --
So it was concealed?
Concealed, yes. And also you could bring your own bottle in.
Hip flasks.
Sit it down on the floor.
Yes. Now at the Dreamland there were some performers, do you remember Billie Ledman?
I don't remember Billie Ledman, no. I heard of him.
Ralph Delaney?
I heard the name, also.
Now what about Snow Fisher?
Yes, I knew Snow Fisher very well.
Really?
Yes.
Now he was supposed to be a great cakewalk man?
He was supposed to be the greatest of the cakewalkers, yes. And that strutting, they call it the same thing, strutting. You know.
Uh-huh.

He was an expert strutter and cake-walker. I knew Snow Fisher very well, he was famous in his day. He was a goodlooking kid, you know, real, real dark. Real fine dresser. He dressed -- he was one of the best dressers of all male entertainers, during his time.
Well, how would he dress?
Well he would dress, you know, at that time, they had the style was a pinch back, pinch back
style, you know the coats with the wide lapels and the mid-section was tight and they had pleats in the back.
Uh-huh.
And bellbottomed pants. And high waisted trousers.
What colors would it be?
Well, he would wear white, he liked to dress in white.
Uh-huh.
And then you know naturally tuxedos, everything would be in the same style with his spats and everything. Patent leather shoes. Very fine dresser.
And he just did a dance?
That's all he did, a dance act, yes.
Uh-huh.

He sang and one of his famous numbers was, 'Shine.' He did, 'Shine.' That was one of his popular songs that he did, he would strut to, so he could strut to his cane, high hat and all that -- silk hat,
Uh-huh. Now why was he famous, was he -- did he become famous at the Dreamland?
Well he -- yes, he was a very popular in Chicago.
Uh-huh.
He had a air about him that, you
know, a personality -- a beautiful smile, very nice looking boy, and he had an air about him that the people liked. When he performed, you know, you could tell he was really first class.
Uh-huh.
There was nothing -- you couldn't say anything bad about Snow Fisher. Beautiful white teeth, you know?
Uh-huh.
He was just out of sight, he was very popular in Chicago.
What ever happened to him?
Well he went to Europe, you know. I think that's -- I think he died inEurope and he was a sensation in Europe, for years. In the '20's.
Uh-huh.
Late '20's, he died I think in Europe, I think so. He was very, very popular inEurope, played the best of clubs.
Did you ever see him, was he over there, did you seehim over there?
I saw him over there, also, yes.
When you with Sam?
With Sam Wooding,yes, yes. He was a big shot in Paris, big, big shot in Paris.
But he didn't perform with the Chocolate Kitties?
No, I don't remember, not when I was with the band, maybe before, he never performed with them.
What about Olive Hickman?
Olive Hickman, I didn't know Olive Hickman.
You heard of her?
No. I don't remember that name at all.
Now did you ever go to the Pekin Inn?
Yes.
What was that like, was it a Chinese place?

It was a Chinese place, yes. It was a joint where the musicians would gather there quite a lot and they would have a few players, sometimes would play the Pekin Inn. But it was mostly a Chinese -- where you get good Chinese food.
Now that was common in those days, wasn't it --
Oh, yes.
-- to have black music in Chinese places?
Right, that's right. Yes. Very
common.
joints.
And what were they called, chopsuey
Well, yes. Well the Pekin Inn, they didn't call themselves a chopsuey place at all, it was just the Pekin Inn.
Uh-huh.
It was very popular, quite a lot of the musicians would go to meet at the Pekin Inn, after hours.
Uh-huh.
And some time they had 4 little playing sessions there.
Now were these places, like the Pekin, were they run by Chinese people?
I -- that I don't really know. You never knew who ran a lot of the clubs in Chicago, at that time.
Uh-huh.

But I have an idea that the mob, you know the people, the gangsters, or whatever you all them, had a lot to do with most all the clubs in Chicago. At that time, cause they were supplying, you know, beer and stuff to all of them, see, they probably ran them.
Were you ever involved in -- was there ever a time in your career, where the mob affected what you did?

Well, no, I don't think they affected, and I was in a raid once in the Dreamland, that's all I remember and nothing happened, you know, money would straighten out everything in those days. But I was in a raid in Chicago, and I remember the Capone -- members of the Capone organization come in all the time. You could tell when they came into a club, cause they were big spenders, and they just practically came in and locked the door and they took charge of the night. You know, they'd close it for the night for their own entertainment.
Uh-huh.

They were very nice tippers, and the band stayed after hours, they'd come at 3:00 o'clock or 4:00, we'd stay there till sunup, play for them. We came out with quite a nice little pocket-ful of money. During that time.
So they really liked the music?
Oh they did, oh sure, well I think if it wasn't for the Capone organization I don't think the clubs would've existed in Chicago at that time.
What about Mae Brady, did you know her?
I didn't know Mae Brady.
Did you know of her?
That name seems to ring a bell.
She was a violinist and she had a
band at the Dreamland for awhile, but it was probably before you came.
That was before, I guess.
Yes. And then, there was another violinist, Elliott Washington.
I remember that name, yes. I remember that name, Elliott Washington, yes.
What about a pianist named Bertha [Gonzalez]?
I didn't know Bertha [Gonzalez], no.
She was with Oliver.
Is that so? I didn't know her. No.
Now, I think that more or less covers it. Are there any other people you remember from that time, that maybe that I didn't bring up?
Well, I did mention George Dewey Washington and George Richardson, didn't I?
No.

Well they were -- I thought I did. They were great singers. They were the two -- Walter Richardson. They were the two most popular male singers in Chicago at that time. And they sang at the Dreamland and they were singing at the Vendome Theater and Metropolitan Theater and other clubs, they'd go from club to club. Singing, maybe
a few days at the Sunset, a week a the Vendome. They were the two most popular male singers in Chicago at that time.
Now, records, how important were records to a band, for instance?

Well they weren't too popular in those days. Recording was just -- it was hard to get a recording, because they weren't buying records in those days, other than say Mame Smith records. Mame Smith I think sold more records than any of the singers. During that time. I think before Bessie, maybe.
Uh-huh.

Sold more records than any of them. And until Louie started recording with his Hot Five. Now after he started, then records sales started going up. Then other groups started recording, also. Jimmy Noon sold a lot of records too. But not as many as Armstrong did. Cause records weren't too popular. Not jazz records, not until that time. Of course, Johnny Dunn, he sold -- he was I think -- he was the first jazz hit record recording. That I know about.
But records -- lot of performers didn't get paid a lot of money for making records?
Oh, no, you didn't get paid very much.
I was wondering whether they looked on the records as sales tools, in other words if you had a recording out, didn't that increase that -- your chance of

getting good bookings? I don't think so. I really don't think so. Now of course Fletcher Henderson had a lot of recordings, then. They're -- weren't too many of them bought. They didn't sell too many of them. I don't think they had anything to do with it at all, not like today. Records didn't mean that much to --

I noticed in going through the black papers of the time, like the Chicago Defender, whenever they talked about blues, this is in the '20's, in their reviews or articles, they're always talking about the women.
Right, that's true.
They never talk about th e men and if it weren't for the ads, for the records, you wouldn't know that male blues singers existed.
Right, that's right.
Why do you supposed that was?
Because the males -- I don't think there were any male blues singers. I don't remember any.
There were lots of them.
Now that may have been, but I don't remember any of them. I remember -- I have heard a lot of male blues singers in the South.
Uh-huh.
Most of them were guitar players,
also, they played guitar and sang the blues. But I don't remember any real popular blues singer, a male blues singer during that time. I don't.
No, they were sort of neglected.
Neglected, yes. Cause blues singers, you know, they were Mame Mammie Smith and all the rest of them.
They didn't appear. The male blues singers, apparently did not appear on stage.
They didn't I don't remember any of them. Any of them. They were in the background.
Right. Now what about male singers singing with the bands. Today, most -- well a lot of instrumentalists who also sing, they don't take that side of it seriously, but they'll sing anyway.
Yes.
And I know, for instance, on some of the old Jimmy Noon records, where Junie C. Cobb would do a vocal or something.
Yes.
Was Louie the first singing star of the --
I think he was, oh yes he was. Al Williams did some singing too. New Orleans type singing. Yes he did.
I recorded Al Williams in 1961.
Is that so?
He was singing then.
Yes, he did some singing with Sam Woodings band on some of the records that we did.
Uh-huh. And of course, Earl Hines and Money Cara --
Yes.
-- and people were doing some little back-up singing there.
Right, yes, that's true, yes.
Now, who would you say in the '20's, in Chicago, and let's see -- let's determine what years you were in Chicago.
Now who were the really big stars?
Well the big stars were -- well now, let's see now. Course, we mentioned Alberta Hall and Trixie Smith was a big star then. During that time, too.
Alberta Hunter, yes.
Alberta Hunter and Trixie Smith, were the big stars --
Of the singers?
Yes.
Uh-huh.
I think Ethel Waters, I think --

I don't know. I don't know about Ethel Waters, I don't know whether she was around there at that time. But they had singers that came through there with the Whitman Sisters that were very popular. They were -- Princess White was one of them. And course, that was another thing, the TOB shows had a lot of them.
Princess White just died, didn't she?
Yes, she died just -- I was on that concert when she died.
She died on concert?
Yes. Yes, we had a concert up in New York state somewhere, outside of Larchmont.
Uh-huh.
And she died right after singing her two songs.
She was about -- well she was in her 80's.
Well she was 95.
Oh she was -- right, 95.
Right.
How was she singing?
Well she sang very well. She sang all of her songs, the last song was 'Peeping Through the Keyhole.' That was the last song, she sang it without any prob-

lem at all. And she finished singing and said she -- she was very well received and she told her audience today I'm 95 years old and says I feel a little tired, I have a lot of butterflies in my stomach and she walked off the stage, sat down and died.
Now, okay getting back to 1926 and Chicago. How did musicians in Chicago regard New York, was that the --
They didn't.
They didn't?
No, they did not. No.
There was no big dream of getting to New York?

No big dream of getting to New York at all. Because New York was entirely different type of -- their music was entirely different. And it didn't have the feeling of the music in Chicago. It was more sophisticated.
Uh-huh.
More classical than the music in Chicago.
Course Louie had gone to New York and was a sensation.
He was a sensation.
And that didn't make the other people want to go.

No. they wanted him to come back and they welcomed him back. That was another trumpet player there -- was very popular there by the name of Reuben Reeves Rubin Reed. He was popular in Chicago during the time Louie was away.
Uh-huh.

And they had -- they had Rubin Reed Reuben Reeves went away and when he returned, they had banners on all the cars, almost -- not all the cars, but quite a lot of cars up on the South Side, at that time, welcoming Rubin Reed Reuben Reeves back to Chicago. And they had a big display and a lot of bally-hoo about Rubin Reed Reuben Reeves, and when he came back to Chicago he was at the Metropolitan Theater with -- oh, what's that name. You know the band if I thought of it. He was at the Metropolitan for a long time, Sammy Stewart's band.
Uh-huh.

And they had all the bally-hoo they could get together at that time to welcome Rubin Reed Reuben Reeves back to Chicago. Shortly, almost the same time they did the same thing with Louie Armstrong, so that was I think a little feeling between the -- I mean not on Louie's side, but I don't think Reuben Rubin cared too much for Louie Armstrong's popularity. I don't think so. But Louie came just maybe say on the tailend of Rubin Reed's Reuben Reeves return and then you didn't hear anymore of Rubin Reed Reuben Reeves.
Hum.
No more. Cause Louie came back and he upset the whole place.
Did you ever hear Bessie Smith?
Did I? I played with Bessie Smith.
Where did you play?
I played with Bessie Smith at the Bijou Theater when she came there.
Oh, that's right you mentioned that.

I played with Bessie Smith, sometimes she would have a piano, sometimes she didn't. It depended upon the finances. As I said before, lot of the blues singers when they could afford to carry pianos with them, they did. But sometimes they couldn't because they didn't have the money, they were in arrears with the -- you know -- the --
But when was this, that you played with Bessie Smith?

Well, I played with Bessie at the Bijou Theater. I was in the pit, cause we had to play -- a lot of times we had to play with singers and sometimes we didn't. And most the times, when they'd bring a pianists, they wouldn't use a pit band at all.
Uh-huh.
But when they didn't have a piano player, why we had to play. Maggie Hargraves was one of the finest of all show piano players and blues piano players alive
at that time. She could play with anyone. Well I played with Bessie -- the year I don't remember. It couldn't of been in '25. I could've been somewhere around '25. Late '25.
Well, if it was '25, then surely Bessie could've afforded a pianist at that time, right, she was very big at that time.

Well, she was big, yes, but you'd be surprised at the times when they were -- as I said before this was all money. They came through there some of them, well the TOBA was the only way of making a living. And it was rough, because they wasn't getting paid, half the time. Lot of times they couldn't afford a piano player.
And there was some piano players that just went along with them, worked with Bessie or the rest of the piano players just for expenses because they couldn't do any better themselves.
Uh-huh.
They would get their hotel, food and afew dollars. There were times when those other blues singers were in destitute circumstances. Including Bessie Smith.
Do you remember people like Bootsy Swann?
Oh, I remember Bootsy Swann.
And Pearl Swann?
Yes.
Pearl Swann, she's still around.
Is that so?
Yes, yes.
Oh, yes, I remember them well.
They were husband and wife?
Yes.
Comedy team, were they not?
Yes. Yes.
And I know they toured with Bessie at one point.
Uh-huh.
But I guess they were very popular on the whole TOBA circuit.
They were very popular, yes.
And [Hootan and Hootan?]
[Hootan and Hootan] yes. Yes.
Didn't they do sort of a preaching --

Yes, it was sort of a preaching thing, yes. And I remember -- I think they started -- I don't know, I didn't know Johnny Hudgins Hodges until I went to Europe with Sam Hudgins. But I think they started that type of thing that Johnny Hodges was doing.
Well Johnny Hudgins Hodges, of course, was also doing a lot of writing for the Defender, wasn't he?
I didn't know that.
He had a regular --
Yes, he did.
-- column.
Yes he did, yes. He certainly did.

And he had this pantomine when he used the trumpet all the time, in fact, his act, you couldn't hardly -- you wouldn't be able to do his act, if he couldn't find a trumpet player to play his act with it.
Did you ever play with him?
Oh yes. I've played with Johnny Hodges, yes.
Hudgins
And --
I played with him in Europe, with Sam Wooding, he went on the tour with us.
Uh-huh.
And I played all of his wa-wa- things, he -- his pantomine things.
Well, what kind of act was that?

Well, he was a black-faced comedian, and he didn't say a thing. Just came out, with a Bert Williams type of costume on, black face and everything he did was pantomine and the trumpet player was supposed to play every movement he made. When he opened his mouth to say something, the trumpet player would naturally play with the plunger, you know he had it all -- it was all arranged. And every movement he made was done with the trumpet. He's singing a song, we play

like, wow-wow- things. Wow-wow-wow-wow. And then he's stop the opening number and wow-wow-wow-wow. And we would -- it was like a trumpet talking thing behind the stage, playing his whole act with him, because his act without the trumpet player he couldn't make it. Joe Smith, I think, was the first to do that with it, I think. Either Joe or -- yes, I think Joe. Was the first.
I guess comedians were very important in those days?

They were, yeah. Certainly, they were very, very important. A show without a comedian, was no show at all. And Johnny Hodges was very famous, very popular -- he stayed -- and also in Europe, he stayed in Europe many years. He was very, very popular, made a lot of money.
Did comedians also perform in the clubs, like at Dreamland --
Oh, yes, comedians performed in the clubs there.
What about the people like Butterbeans and Susie?
Well, Butterbeans he -- yes, they did a lot of night club work in Chicago, they were very popular, too. They were headliners. Butterbeans and Susie.
Uh-huh.
Yes, I played their act so many, many
times. And another famous act by the name of Brown and McGraw. Did you ever hear of them?
No.

They had a dance act, very fast dance act and I think their act lasted almost an hour. They also couldn't -- their act depended on the help of a trumpet player. Louie Armstrong was the first one to play that act. And Louie, in fact, made Brown and McGraw famous because their act was nothing without a trumpet. He blew them to death. Louie played to death for that act. Everything they did, Louie Armstrong was right on with the trumpet. So, after that, when they went out without Louie they had to have a trumpet player that could play. I mean when you got through with Brown and McGraw you were ready to go to the hospital, cause they would kill you.
They had everything written out.
This is Browning and McGraw?
Brown and McGraw.
Brown and McGraw.
Two people, man and wife. And they're very fast dance act. All was done with a trumpet player. So you had to go on the stage and play with them.
And what sort of dance would they do?
Well, it was a fast, dance like it was I think it was before the jitterbug.
Was it acrobatic?
Acrobatic and jazz. Oh, acrobatic, yes.
Was it something like the -- Nicholas Brothers?
Charleston and the tap and everything yes, all combined.
The splits?
The splits and everything, throw her all around and very fast type of dance act. But they depended on the trumpet. Trumpet player, very important part of that act.
Now of course there were no P.A. systems in those days.
No P.A. systems. They didn't need it because the acoustics of the theater were good enough, I think in those days.
Yes, now what about -- did you ever perform tent shows, or did I ask you that before?
Yes, I did a tent show, I did one, in Kentucky.
I had wondered about it because in a tent, of course you don't have the acoustics with the --
No acoustics, that's why it was very hard on musicians to play tent shows. Cause you had to play so loud. All the time. Very, very difficult tent shows. And
I didn't last too long doing that kind of work.
And how were the tent shows lit?
Well, they had a light -- they had electric lights. Electric lights in tent shows.
And I know Ma Rainey had a a generator in her bus.
I guess so.
There were some poor tent shows, the Silas Green show wasn't --
Well they went back to the kerosene lights, too. You know. In a lot of the tent shows. I've seen lot of -- come through Nashville there, kerosene lights. I can remember that very well.
Uh-huh.
Kerosene lights with the reflectors.
Was there much jealousy -- backstage jealousy in those shows?
Well, yes. There was a certain amount of that, you know, the stars and the soubrettes, as they called them. There was quite a lot of jealousy going on. Always, even among chorus girls.
Uh-huh.
Fights and things like that. And, we can go back to medicine shows, you know, did you ever hear for -- about the medicine shows?
Oh, sure.
I played a medicine show one, quite a few of them, yes.
What were they like?

Well, you see, there was the big wagon that'd pull up -- in the back of the wagon they let the tail down and set up curtains in the back, you know, draped the back with curtains and they'd have a comedian. Now these comedians most of them were very good comedians, and dancers, and joke tellers. And they sang a lot. Along the Johnny Hudgins type of a singer. Course, it wasn't pantomine, but they did -- had some of the best comedians, back in those days on medicine shows. It was a very good job.

And then, of course, the guys that were selling the medicine, naturally, he was white. A very good talker. Very good talker, he would sell his product. I remember one time they had a -- they were selling some kind of a glass that was made out of peppermint of some kind. This glass. And they would sell this glass, I guess maybe 50¢ or something 25¢ or 50¢, it was supposed to cure a lot of things and you poured water in it and then the water would, you know, take the taste of peppermint. From the glass. And it was supposed to be good for rheumatism and all that. And they sold a lot of that.
And so eventually you used up the
glass.

Oh, yes. Well, you know, after the show, you cut out cause the glass would probably disintegrate, or something, or warp or something. And they had snake oil, and all kind of -- for arthritis and rheumatism and they had bottles of bird medicines, for different type of ailments. Even tuberculosis they had things. And they did a big business. the talkers were very good confidence men. They would sell a lot of those bottles course the show would be first. Put the show on first. And some of them had tambourines and it was a minstrel type of entertainment. They would have on the back of these medicine wagons.
Now some of the people you performed with, when you were very young, must've been up in age then, they must've been people who really were from the former century, right?
They were up in age, that's right.
And what -- did their attitude, was there a generation gap, there? Were they considered old-fashioned, minstrel people?

No, they weren't considered old fashioned, not at that time, because that was the thing, minstrel shows and medicine wagons. That was the thing of the day. I wouldn't -- they weren't considered old fashioned at all. Cause people would look forward to these shows. Especially

medicine shows. Cause they had very good entertainment and I think some of our famous comedians doing their time on that medicine minstrel show -- that started out on medicine minstrel shows. Lot of them played washboards, and tambourines and they danced, told jokes, sang. I don't think they were considered -- no they weren't considered old fashioned because that was the thing during that time.
And how did you travel around?

Oh a lot of that stuff I did in Nashville, itself. The only tent show I played wound up in Kentucky. In the coal mines area. But I didn't stay because my lip split wide open. After a couple of days I had to leave, I just went back home. I couldn't play a -- that tent. I was too young and that was for a hard core, that thing -- there was a trumpet player with me on that show he'd been on that show and he had hardened himself to it. But I could never remember this guy's name, but he was expert carnival, that's all he did was play the -- those type of shows. But I couldn't do it I was too young and I wasn't strong enough to play, so I stayed about two days and I had to go back to Nashville, I couldn't take it. But it was good experience though. But not for me.
But all of this was good experience, wasn't it?
All experience.
Kind of
Any experience that young musicians today just don't get.

That's right they don't get that, no. And course Nashville being away from everything. That's all they had there, carnivals and medicine shows and minstrel shows. It was just constantly playing in Nashville.
Now, in Chicago, was there a lot of sitting in, lot of jam sessions and after hours?
Yes, after hours, yes.
Going on?
Oh, there was a lot of that.
And then where was this, where did this take place?
Well, there was a club there that we used to sit in up to the Apex Club, at times.
Where Jimmy Noon played?
Yes. And they came by the Dreamland at times. At times the Dreamland was loaded with musicians, playing.
Do you remember Richard Morgan?
No.
He was in the '30's, he became -- he became Bessie Smith's lover, he was a bootlegger in Chicago in the '20's.
No, I didn't know him. I read about
him, but I didn't know him.
Now he used to throw parties and have musicians coming in and performing and --
Yes, I guess so --
-- was there much of that do you remember private individuals, bootleggers?
Oh, yes. There were lot of rent parties going on in Chicago at that time.
Uh-huh.

Rent parties and card games. Performers and musicians would meet all the time. And apartments, and where the bootleg whiskey was sold and cards and gambling, that's where a lot of the people made their money to pay their rent.
Right.
They served chittlings and things like that, barbecued ribs, chicken, fried chicken.
What about --
That was very prevalent up in Chicago.
What about buffet flats?
Well, buffet flats, I never got too interested in, in fact I was afraid to attend a lot of those places because lot of those places were raided, very often.
Uh-huh.
You know, cause there was a lot of

home made whiskey made. Now where I stayed in Chicago, the lady where I stayed she made home made gin. But she was lucky she was never raided, but that was going on almost in every -- not in every apartment, but many of the apartments in Chicago, everybody made their own whiskey. And, naturally, there were a lot of raids because they were running competition through the mob.
Right.
Raids every night. Chicago.
Was there a difference between a buffet flat and a good time flat?
I don't think there was any differ-ence. At all.
The same thing.
The same, thing, yes.
And now these places, were they just places, where everything illegal went on?

Well, I don't know about everything. But I know there was gambling and food and whiskey, home made whiskey. I know that.
