And a lot of the entertainers, the -- especially the women, the older women entertainers, ran a lot of these places because they were very popular in show business and you go about such and such a house after the -- to eat and naturally there was whiskey there. Home made whiskey and that was widely done in Chicago, during those
days, cause everybody you know the drinkers would like to go somewhere where they could drink, after hours.
But when you played a rent party, was that -- were you paid for that?
I never played a rent party.
You never did.

But I would go by a few of them, because I had a -- one of the girls who was dancing at the Dreamland, took me to a rent party once. I never played there, I don't think there was any -- I don't remember any bands playing at a rent party. It was mostly recordings like blues singer, like Mame Smith was in everybody's apartment. During that time, maybe a few Ma Rainey's but Mame Smith -- everybody had a recording of Mame Smith. And that was all you would hear in a rent party. At rent parties, because everybody was busy drinking --
I've often wondered about that, you know, because as you see I have an old victrola here.
Uh-huh.
And you don't get a lot of volume on an old victrola, and if you had a room with a lot of people, I don't see how you could hear the music.
Oh, you could hear it because they made some very fine record machines in those days. Remember when Victor came out with a small one. I remember and every-
body would buy a portable and it was very, very loud.
Uh-huh.

Very, very loud, oh yes. They were very, very loud. I bought one myself. And oh yes, I think there was a fellow named UnionJack, not Union Jack, but what is the aviator's name? The Black Eagle -- (who) MR. ALBERTSON: Oh, oh, I know you're talking about.
He took the first one to Europe and I went over on the boat with him.
Uh-huh.
He had the first one of those machines. And I went around with him to a couple places, night clubs, we'd sit it on the bar and everybody was so excited to hear such a machine, such volume.
Uh-huh.

Of course, they didn't have the volume that they have today in those days, Victor put out a very nice machine, everyone was buying them. And course they played the records at these rent parties and you'd,-- well that was like background music. I don't think anybody was paying too much attention, because everybody was talking and drinking.
Uh-huh.
You know. And eating chicken. Chicken was very, very popular in all those rent parties, fried chicken. And home made booze. And Mamie's Smith's [record] was played every-
Uh-huh.
Everybody had those records, 'Muggles' and all that.
What about the Bert Williams records?
Well Bert Williams records were mostly in the homes of people.
Uh-huh.
You didn't hear those out in places like that. But everybody, almost everybody that had a machine in those days had Bert Williams records, all of them.
Now you recorded for Paramount when you accompanied Ma Rainey and you were playing the soprano sax then, wasn't that an unusual instrument you were playing?
Well, it was a very unusual instrument, but that was my first instrument and I thought I played it very well, in fact, everybody liked the way I played the soprano saxophone.
Uh-huh.

And I couldn't -- it was very difficult for me to play clarinet, that's why I played soprano, I couldn't learn the clarinet at all. So I learned the soprano saxophone and I played it -- I was -- I played it in the style of clarinet, fast running styles like Jimmy Noon and
Barney Bigard, I played that type on the soprano saxophone, and it was very well received everywhere.
Do you remember what the was -- the studio was like, Paramount?
Yes, well this was a pretty beat-up looking place. It was more like a loft type of place, very beat up. It wasn't anything beautiful about it.
Uh-huh.
It was just a storeroom type of a place. I would say, with a big microphone, we played through the megaphone --
The horn.
The horn, yes.
Only one horn?
Only one horn, yes.
And I supposed Ma Rainey stood in front of that horn?
Yes, she stood in front of the horn, the band was back of her.
Uh-huh, and who else was in that band?

Well, I remember Gerald Hobson on trumpet and Sallis White, I think, on bass, and Jimmy Flowers trumpet, the banjo player, I don't -- I can't remember his name. He was a very fine boy. But I don't remember -- and
we had Thigpen, I think, was on the drums. Ed Thigpen.
Ed Thigpen?
Yeah, he was Al Winn's drummer.
The same Ed Thigpen who was with Oscar Peterson?
Oh, that's his son.
Ed Thigpen, Sr., I see. I didn't know he --
Oh yes. Well Thigpen was also a drummer with Andy Kirk for years.
OH, right, right, of course. And, so that was your first record, I guess you didn't -- you didn't hear that until it came out.
I didn't hear that record until 1967, in London.
When John Chilton played it for you?
Yes.
But other records you did hear?

Oh, yes, you know, I bought quite a few records, I had one of those machines, but the 78's would break so easily, you know. You was always breaking them. You just got tired of going buying them over and over again.
Uh-huh. Now, all right so now let's get up to -- we -- where we left off before, you were actually -- you were talking about Latin music you were playing. You
That was Marcelino Guerrero.
Marcelino Guerrero's band, yes that was what from '48 to '50?
Around that time, yes, he had just about the greatest jazz --
Latin?
Latin band. In New York, course most of his musicians were all Americans, other than the rythm section.
Uh-huh.

His saxophone players and had one Cuban trumpet player, Hot Lips Garcia, and myself. But we were the soloists. (well, sort of.) No, I played lead in that band. Garcia was the soloist. But the saxophone section -- was all American. Had Joe Hayman in there, Greeley Walton, and this guy that -- I forget his name now. They had a great saxophone section, and all American, they had a certain amount -- the writers would write mostly swing music for the band.
Uh-huh.

And the arrangments, but the Cubans they had band before Machito, they had the greatest swing band in New York at that time. So I worked with that band, for awhile, because they weren't getting too much work and that's what I went with Machito for -- show for awhile and

I was fired out of that band because I couldn't play the -- couldn't get the -- couldn't synchronize myself with the rhythm, because he had a different type of band than Machito, he was more authentic Cuban band.
Uh-huh.

So, I didn't stay there, that's when I met Wilbur DeParis, in fact I joined Wilbur DeParis as a -- I did a lot of work as a substitute for Sidney. Cause he would take off a lot, he was involved in a religious thing, and he would take off a lot and so I started playing with Wilbur DeParis' band at that time.
But you also -- in '51 you toured with -- you went back with Calloway, didn't you?
Went back with Calloway, yes.
And you toured what --
Well --
In this country --
We had a few one night stands with Calloway.
Oh, is that all it was?
One night stands, yes.
Uh-huh.
We went to Montevideo with Calloway, and Uruguay, we were down there I guess a few weeks. With Cab Calloway and after we came back we did a few one night

stands he didn't make any money at all, it was a bad one, it was rock and roll, I'd say was coming in during that time, and they were taking all the business all the crowds, we'd play places in the South the same night they had rock and roll, and Cab didn't have anyone at his dances so he couldn't keep that band going.
So then you went to Boston, is that right, or did something happen in between?

Yes. Well, I went with Cab, it was '51. To South America. We came back. '52 I went back down there with Perez Prado. And Paul Webster and myself were the trumpet players the featured trumpet players with Perez Prado's band. We went over the same, played the same carnival in Montevideo that Cab -- that we did with Cab, so after that we played Brazil and a few places with Prado. And then when we left Prado in Argentina. That's where I met my wife.
In Argentina?
My last wife. Present wife.
Is she Argentinian?

She's Argentinian. I left Perez Prado, there. We played Santiago, Chile, he also had Michael -- Gene Michael in the band. Saxophone player. Gene Michael was a famous first lead man, with Cecil's band. He was in that band. Gene Michael, Paul Wilson and myself were -- went in that band together. And then we came back to -- because

we weren't getting paid. Perez Prado, he didn't pay us off and he had a lot of money problems with the band and so we broke up and -- inSantiago, Chile. And came back to New York. Now that was the end of Perez Prado as far as we were concerned. Course he continued on with his band and I did a lot of work -- that's when I started work -- doing subs for Wilbur's band. Gigging around at other little places I could get.
Uh-huh. But-- so this is all before you went to Boston. Did you go to Boston with Vic Dickenson?
Well I went to Boston, yes, that was before. No, that was 1952.
Yeah.
Cause that was after Perez Prado, then I went to Boston with Vic Dickenson at the Mahogany Hall.
And you were there for quite a while.
Oh, for at least a year. And my son was born during that time there, Boston.
Uh-huh. You really were living in Boston?
Living in Boston, yes.
Now what about -- you were -- you led a band for Wilbur DeParis, didn't you?
Well, he -- yes, he would decide that he would like to have a second band. I don't know why but I guess he had an idea he wanted to monopolize Dixieland
you know, thing. And he organized a second band and I think the second band was course, better than his band, original band. It was coming to that point.
Who was in that band?
Well I think Lee Blair was in that band. And let me see, who the heck was in -- see I'd have to sit down and think about that because it didn't last that long for me to remember who was in that band.
I see. Was it here in New York?
No, it was in Boston.
Well, that was in Boston?

We rehearsed here and he sent the band to Boston and the band was so great and he came up there one night and he come up there to pay off. He come all the way to Boston to collect the money to pay the band off. The band was so great he decided to disband it.
Okay, so --
I have an idea that George Stevenson was in that band --
Trombone player?
Yes. Clarinet player, who the heck was that, I'll have to check on that.
And that was called Wilbur DeParis and his orchestra.
That's right, Wilbur DeParis --
But that band never recorded?
No we didn't record the band at all.
Uh-huh.
He disbanded it right away.
And how long did that last?
I think about three weeks.
Oh, is that all?
That's all. Because the band was shaping up very good and I think he -- it was rumored that he didn't want that competition.
This was in what year?
That was -- gosh let me see, gosh that was after the Mahogany Hall, that must've been about '53 or something like that.
Uh-huh. So you were still with -- weren't you with Vic Dickenson from '52 to '55?
'52 I was with Vic Dickenson -- I think it was just only two years.
Yeah.
That we stayedup in Boston, maybe not that long, closer to two -- at least a year.
I see.
It was every bit of a year, but not too much over a year.
Now you -- so then you went back into
then you went into the regular Wilbur DeParis band?
Yes, as a sub. Yes.
Yes. And you went to Africa with Wilbur DeParis?
I went to Africa with Wilbur DeParis.
Was that your first trip toAfrica?
First trip to Africa, yes.
How was that trip?
That was a very good trip. Very fine, very, very well received trip. The band was a sensation. In Africa.
Uh-huh. And now what did you hear, you must've heard some African music?
Oh yes, they entertained us most every country. We heard the best of their groups. We heard the bands played -- where they played cow horns on -- the entire band played horns, horns from the cow.
Uh-huh.

I guess -- I called it cow, but it was these horns and they would play, they would -- this was inUganda, where they had this King of the -- of Uganda, he had several bands. He had bands where they had nothing but horns, horns from the cows, and then he had a band that played all drums. And each one of these bands had their own tent. Where they played all over the grounds of his palace. He had
all kinds of drums, he had drums so big that you couldn't hardly -- you couldn't move them they were so big.
Did you play with any African bands?

No, we didn't play with them, no. Because I don't think we could've. They couldn't of played with us and we couldn't play with them. But it was typical -- they'd have drum concerts. Then they'd have this vibraphone kind of bands, they had bands that were nothing but vibraphones.
Vibraphone or marimbas?

Marimbas, and that's all they played, they had their own music, that we couldn't of played with them. The only place we played a little with them was on -- I played with them was on a radio show in Nairobi, that was when with Herb Mann, I have a recording of that.
Oh, you do?
Entire show, yes.
So that was '57, and you went to Africa with Wilbur. And then you were still with Wilbur in 1960, you went to Europe?
Yes, I went to Europe with him.
Course, inbetween all this you were making records, like I know you did a -- you were on that album Juanita Hall did of Bessie Smith songs.
Yes, yes.
And that surprised me, at that time.
Juanita Hall singing blues like that.

Yes, everybody was surprised at Juanita singing -- I also was in, I think, I worked at went to the Jack Silverman's International Club there with a Latin trio in around '56. And I stayed maybe quite a few years. And then --
According to Chilton's book you led your own band at the International --
Well I went in there --
From '60 to '65.

Yes, I was in there with Alvarez, Enrico Alvarez. We played dance music, and of course Mike Durso had the show band, he played the dance music. That was only a trio, trumpet, bass -- or quartet, trumpet, bass, piano and drum. And Alvarez decided to go -- move to Puerto Rico, so during that time, when he left, well the whole band was going but Jack Silverman wanted me to stay. And I didn't want to stay because I said, I'm not Latin, I wouldn't fill the spot, so he said, well get some Latin musicians. So I did, I stayed there and I got a Latin drummer and a Latin piano player, was only three of us, no bass.
Uh-huh.
And I stayed there for quite a long time with that trio. [PAUSE]
And --
And also I was involved with Wilbur
But you also went to Europe with Sammy Price, didn't you?
Yes, I was with Sammy Price and I think that was in '58.
Uh-huh.
We made a tour over there.
And you went to Africa with Herbie Mann in 1960?
Right.
So you did quite a bit of travelling?
Did quite a lot of travelling. Yes.
During that time. And, now so this band at the International was really just a trio.
It was a trio, that's all.
It was Latin dance music?
Latin dance music. We played some American thing.
I see. Now you also worked with Benny Goodman in the mid-'60's, I guess it was after that, May , '66, to January --
May '67. And wasn't that, was that difficult?
Well, no, it wasn't difficult. Be-

cause first thing he had -- he auditioned me. He and Hank Jones, they auditioned me somwhere on the East Side, and he set back there in his chair and I just whatever I wanted to play, Hank played it with me and he listened. And he says okay. He liked me. So, I went out on gigs with him. Jobs with him. I went to Brussels with him. At the fair, I guess it was -- the festival.
This wasn't when Jimmy Rushing was with --
No, Jimmy wasn't --
This wasn't the world's fair?
No it was festival, jazz festival, at Brussels at the time.
Uh-huh.
I worked with him there, I went to -- worked with him in quite a lot of places, in Chicago, and concerts he had there. Connecticut, worked a lot --
Uh-huh.
It wasn't difficult -- In Miami we played at the Americana, not the Club there, I forget the name of the club.
You did not find him difficult to work with?
I didn't find Benny difficult, no but he's a super star and I think he's very hard to please at

times, there're times when he -- he feels like that he's not satisfied with the -- his musicians. That's the way it appeared tome. And he would get irritated at certain times. You know, and I guess that's because he's such a great player that it affects you that way. But he and I got along very well together, I think.
Now after you left Goodman, you went back to Europe in '67, with something called Top Brass, what was that?
Yes. Oh, that was a terrific -- that was a great tour, 15 days.
Uh-huh.

We had Nat Pierce, drummer, I never remember his name. The had a trio that Benny Morton and myself played -- the same trio played with Clark Terry and Bobby Brookmeyer. And then Maynard Ferguson's big band was on the program. And Benny Morton and myself sat in with Maynard's big band. Just for kicks, we didn't get paid for it but we I guess it saved Maynard a couple of salaries. But we did it, we volunteered to do it. His -- you know, he agreed, that he was happy to have us, so we played with his big band and during all the -- cause as I said, we did our act, we went on first, then Clark Terry and Bobby Brookmeyer, second and Maynard Ferguson closed the bill. And then during the time Maynard Ferguson and Clark Terry were playing jam sessions together,
We were in the big band, so we didn't get out there and get in the jam session at all. But it was a very nice tour, and a tour up and down the coast and back.
Now all this time did you -- when did you start playing with Ricardo Rey's band?
After that.
After that.
After I left Goodman --
Uh-huh.
-- I went with Ricardo Rey. And --
That was A Latin band, right?
Yes, right. Yes. And I had contracted for this top brass and I left Ricardo to go to England and I came back to Ricardo Rey.
I see and with whom -- Ricardo Rey, you also played Puerto Rico.
Yes I was a soloist in that band, I played all over South America.
Uh-huh. Do you -- you don't play Latin music anymore?

No, I don't because it's conflicting a little bit. I think you have to leave it alone. Although the style of music I played with Ricardo Rey was all American jazz, that I know, that I played with that band. I recorded -- many recordings with Ricardo Rey. It was all done in the
style of music that I play today. It didn't conflict too much
Uh-huh.

-- because it seemed to work itself around with (unintelligible) the band they were all young kids and they knew a lot of -- about jazz from hearing it. But they were Latins and their rhythm was all Latin, all Ricardo--- recordings that I did with that band was strictly jazz solos. The first one I made with him -- with the band called, "Halla-Halla" and the band they had been together quite a few years, I'd say three or four years before and the recording that I made with them of "Halla-Halla" the band went right to the top, they say that that solo was responsible for the band's popularity and he had contracts all over South America. And I had to play "Halla-Halla" four or five times a night. Trumpet solo.
Well did you ever really enjoy playing Latin music, or was it?

I did, with Ricardo Ray, yes. I did because, you see, they could write beautiful things and jazz -- sort of jazz like and then they would turn you loose and let you play alone with the rhythm and all those rhythm and you could play as long as you wanted to play. They don't say the amount of bars, or anything. You could just play anything you wanted to play. And with all that rhythm behind you, I thought it was a great thing. I thought it was great. I
enjoyed it very much.
Now you've had a long career and you've come up through New Orleans music, you've gone through this swing era, through the bop era, --
Uh-huh.
What do you -- ever listen to the music that's going on today, that young people are playing?
All the time, I listen to it all the time, yes.
And, now I know you made a record with Beaver Harris.
Yes.
Who isn't exactly a traditional musician.
No.
You did an album with Beaver Harris, where Maxine Sullivan is on the same album with you. An Album called, 'From Ragtime to No Time.'
Right.
And but what do you think of the music, but what you're playing on that record, is fairly traditional.
Yes. But, and it gets--
And then on the other side of the record, when it gets into no time,
Yes.
It's not very traditional.
That's right.
So, what do you think of that, I know you had a hard time getting into bop music --
Yes, well I tell you --
Even swing.

-- yes, the thing about it, you have to remember that you have to forget -- you have to forget the conventional changes that are played in American traditional music, you have to forget that. And you just have to throw it out of your mind altogether. Because of the music -- the bop type of music that I have been connected with I just -- just -- there's no sort of -- free playing like. There's no eight bars of this, of the and a bridge and right either bars of that. It's mostly free, adlib playing -- you're just on your own. And they have -- the rhythm from the piano are on their own and it's two the way it separate things going at the same time, that's what impressed me. So I didn't find it difficult, although I would rather not do too much of it.
Uh-huh.

Because, I mean, it's pretty hard on your mind to be thinking in that way. You know I'm accustomed to playing something that I know. That I could -- they -- that I have something to follow a guide to go by, a melody or some-
thing, something. But that is difficult
Well now of course -- I would imagine when you hear what is being played today, the music that you didn't quite get with, back then, bop music and swing sounds very, very old fashioned, doesn't it?
Sounds very old-fashioned, that's true. That's true, very, very old fashioned.
So, maybe in a few years this will sound old fashioned --
It will--
-- I don't know where we're getting to.

-- it certainly will, that's the way, that's the cycle they way the thing goes around, it's got to get old fashioned, certainly get old fashioned. You take Dizzy, now, Dizzy Gillespie was one of the greatest, exponents I think of the bebop, type of playing. Then here comes a guy like Clifford Brown, you see what I mean?
Now you like Clifford Brown?
Oh, yes. Then there's quite a few others, Turrentine, whatever his name --
Stanley Turrentine?
And the guy that was killed, what was his name?
Fats Navarro?

Fats Navarro. And see then Dizzy had to move up himself and get, you know, get progressive still. Which he is today, he's very progressive right today. Move up into that -- that is what you call the white trumpet player, what is his name, always in trouble.
Chet Baker.

Chet Baker. See those guys moved up from that and you listen to those real old -- some of those real old bebop records they do sound old fashioned. Compared with what they're playing today. Certainly.
Now there was a period there where Stanley Dance was very active recording [you know] something they call mainstream --
Yeah.
Which you seem to fit into very well. I think you did quite a few recordings during that period, didn't you?
Yes, that's right. Yes.
And mainstream, of course, was just swing, really.
That's all it was, yeah. That's all it was, it was just swing.
With a new name.
All it was. I had a pleasure of playing in Nice, of course the festival, I was thrown in all kind of

groups, I had to play with all kind of bands, there, Earl Hines, British band, German band, a French band and then the last engagement there was very -- was a very interesting group, I -- it was three trumpets, Bobby Hackett, Clark Terry, and myself. And you should've heard that -- you should've heard that.
In 1950, you took another vacation in Europe and, although, I guess it was a vacation, you did some concerts, did you with the Hot Club of France?

Yes. Well, I went to Europe, at that time, mostly to get away, I was having a little matrimonial problem. And I just went to that, I took my horn, said I'm going to stay over there. Something stopped, me the war, no it wasn't the war, I didn't seem -- after I got there, I didn't seem to like it, because I didn't know too many people, and the French musicians, they didn't seem to be very happy about American musicians being over there. I found that true.
Really?

Yes, because I had one of the saxophone players, I met, very fine -- on that engagement that I made played in Nancy, France, for Buck Clayton, Buck had two engagements the same night, one in Nancy and one somewhere else, so that was so many tickets sold, that they sent me to Nancy, to play in Buck's place, and that place was packed, I never saw a place like that, Buck played somewhere else. The manager he was biting his fingernails, he was worried, running (unin-)

looking at around (unintelligible) me, and running around, I don't know what he was talking about, and the musicians all seemed, they were -- they left, in fact they were in one part of the place louder than the other, they didn't socialize with me at all. Even on the train up, there -- one would come and say do you know "Royal Garden Blues?" I say I forgot the "Royal Garden Blues, man, I said, I've been playing it all my life and somebody asked me, do you know this, I says, look, don't worry about the concert, about the music, if that's the type music you're going to play, don't worry about it. But they were all worried, all, man, they were nervous, everyone of them.
And so the manager said, he hoped, he was afraid that he was going to have problems with the box office, giving them the money back. Cause Buck wasn't there.
Uh-huh.

So, he came in, I said look this -- just don't bother me, I said, what are you going to play? So they wrote out some songs, tunes to play, and I know every one of them, and the routines were the standard routines. So, we went out there and the opened up and played, and we played, I forget what we played, but whatever it was, the house came down. The whole place was in an uproar of applause. We did a whole half a concert and while I'm playing good, and solo playing you could hear "come on Buck, come on Buck," all over the place. And at the intermission, the impresario, came out
and announced that Buck Clayton wasn't there, see? That's he's being replaced by Doc Cheatham, something happened, blah, blah, blah, but I got such a round of applause that it didn't matter to the --
So the first part they thought you were Buck?

Yeah, they thought I was Buck Clayton. So we finished the concert and everybody was happy and they had drinks and things, then they came up there and oh, man, they shook my hand almost broke my arm, the musicians they all friends and everthing, they --
Who were these musicians?
I don't know. I don't know any of them, than, Don Byas, was on one of them, he and Bishop, the drummer --
Uh-huh.
-- Wallace Bishop and Don Byas, only two that I can -- the others musicians, I didn't know them and I've never seen them since.
Now when you played with the Hot Club, I guess Django was still alive, wasn't he?
Django was still alive, yes.
Yes. Did you play with Django?
I never played with Django, no.
Did you ever meet him?
I met him, yes. I met him in Paris and I also met him here.
Uh-huh.
But I've never played with -- him.
What do you remember of him?

Well, I only met him, because he -- I didn't -- he hadn't -- didn't ever have too much to say to me because I was just -- he didn't know too much about me. I was just another handshake, I guess. He didn't know much about me, that's the way it appeared, so I naturally I knew about him from all his recordings. I thought he was a great -- I never came in contact with him, kind of a loner type of person, I think. From what I understand. [PAUSE]
Okay, now let's talk about trumpet techniques?
All right.
Talke about what -- I mean you learned to play the trumpet from -- was it N. C. Davis?
Yes.
Now what you learned, how did that differ from what you then learned later from hearing people like Louie Armstrong, how did that differ?
Well, the thing about it -- N. C. Davis was a military man, and he knew how to teach kids, and most of the things we were doing were marches, and we had a

few little simple overtures that we would play, and church music, cause we had to do that because the thing was organized through the Phillips Chapel Church. So we played no -- nothing with jazz in it at all. So naturally we would be jazzing and fooling around on our instruments maybe a few minutes before, at rehearsals before the teacher would come, before Mr. Meredith would come in and then he would resent that very much and bawl us out for playing, you know, dance music or jazz, trying to play it. And that's what broke up the thing.

But, I went to high school -- when I was in high school we had a high school band and we could -- we could play anything but jazz or popular music, dance music. We only had to play marches to bring the kids in the auditorium and take them out. Sometimes we play a little simple something for awhile, someone sang or something, but jazz was looked down on as evil music in those days.

And that's why I went to this Dan Stafford who was at the Barbizon Bijou then he took me out on jobs, he couldn't play but one song and in one key and only two, three fingers, he was a jive artist, but he had a lot of contact with the white people there, they would always use Dan on these jobs at the country club, private homes, and things. And he was a one leg musician and they used to -- when they drank -- they drank a lot of home brew in those days, we played places where we'd have to go out of the house in the back yard to drink home

brew, everybody did it, cause when they take the top off the bottle, it -- the foam would shoot up so high and you couldn't open it in the house, so everybody was in the back yard, drinking home brew. Then when they get drunk round about half way into the dance, then they'd -- there'd be a lot of pistol shooting around the place. Then, you know, Dan, sitting at the piano would stick his leg out and they would take pot shots at Dan's wooden leg, cause they knew he had a wooden leg, so they would shoot at his wooden leg, sometimes they'd hit him, sometimes they'd miss it.

And Dan had a roomful of legs, some of them were all broken and shot up -- we were -- played a private party one day, -- one night and Dan wanted to go up to the men's room, so so they -- he's coming down the steps, cause the men's room -- the bathroom was upstairs, he was coming down the steps with his wooden leg, hopping, and one old guy said, Dan, I'm going to shoot that leg, and Dan said, just as long as you shoot this one and he stick it out and the guy shoot it, bam, and knock the whole bottom off his leg.

But he was well liked, like that. He didn't care. And he made a little extra money, from being a barber, playing around those places. He would take me, and he'd give me a couple of dollars, sometimes, you know, and he didn't -- and as I say, only one song, we would play one song all night long and we played around it. So that was experience right there

that I got, to take one song and play it many different ways. You take a song like, "Rose Room," you can record it under a 1,000 different titles. Or any other song, and record it under so many names, because you've learned to play around it, forget about the melody -- you never go to it at all -- and make up things around the melody. That's the thing that I learned in Nashville.
Just play against the chord.
Yes, play against the chord and you can play a 1,000 different songs.
Now I remember years ago I played trumpet and I took lessons from the first trumpet player with the Danish Symphony Orchestra, and he was in deep shock when I used vibrato.
Right.
Cause that was against all the rules --

Well, I guess in your time -- but in my time vibrato was the thing and I was taught to use vibrato my shaking the hand. Moving the hand back, I do it know, sometimes. And later years they taught it my lip movements, I learned that way, too, but I found that I was cutting my lip. Too much. It wasn't natural. Cause you have to do it natural in the beginning, then it comes natural. But I learned it -- I studied to do it from the lip movement, because in '26, and the jazz trumpet players would -- were using vibrato by shaking
their head up and down. I -- Louis did that, he always did that. You know, shaking his head up and down.
Yeah.

We used to practice that. Shaking our head -- moving our head up and down when we played trumpet, back in the '20's, did that in New York with Shirley Clay, and we worked together at the -- at this dancing school down there. With Bingie Madison's band, I played down there. With Shirley Clay, we used to -- why we practiced shaking our head, playing jazz courses, to get that sound like Louie did.
What about playing, for instance, with the valves half way down? Was when you were first taught by Mr. Davis?
Uh-huh.
Did he teach you that or did you -- did every tone had to be clear?
Every tone had to be clear.
So --
He didn't know anything about jazz. Everything was clear, everything was exact.
Where did you really learn about jazz?
Well that started, as I say, when I got to Chicago, I knew more about it -- was was getting to see what it was all about.
Uh-huh.

There were a few bands that came through Nashville, there, with trumpet players like Ed Swayzee, and Joe Hayman, they came through there with a band called the Clowns, they all had clown suits on. They came through there with a show. And that's the first time I ever heard jazz. Only time was when the travelling bands would come through Nashville and play the Bijou Theater. Then we would sit -- we wouldn't have to play, but we would go in free every night and we'd hear these different bands. Groups. Some very good bands, and that's my first hearing of bands out of -- you know, Nashville, because there was nothing in Nashville -- jazz.
Uh-huh.

We'd get a record, I'd say it was Johnny Dunn, but all of this -- all of this -- the main things that I learned about jazz was in Chicago. When I -- at the end of the show, when the show broke up and I went around -- Little Mitchell, you remember Little Mitchell, hunchback Mitchell?
George Mitchell?
George Mitchell.
Uh-huh.
Guys like that. And all the rest of them. Then I began to hear things.
But before you came to Chicago, you
had heard records? Records, oh yes, Johnny Dunn, and Paul Whiteman, Ted Lewis, that was all.
But did you wonder when you heard those records, did you wonder how they did it?
Yes. I did.
And did you experiment?
I experimented, sure. I -- in fact I copied the exact things that they were doing. I was doing the same thing. Harmon mutes -- the wa-was and all those kind of things, I did all that.

So, by the time you actually got to Chicago and heard this music live, and saw the musicans, the trumpet players on stage or wherever, you had already figured out how they created the various effects, it -- is that it?

Yes, but you did -- they weren't doing the things in Chicago that I had learned, that was all finished, because the things I had learned, that was corny. When I got to Chicago. You wouldn't dare play like that, that do-wacka-do, stuff in Chicago. When I got there. Those are things I learned from the records.
So what -- for instance, what did you learn -- what was the main thing you learned from hearing Louie Armstrong?
The things I learned from Louie Arm-

strong are the things that I heard during discussions that Louis Armstrong had with other musicians at times. I wasn't in on it, but I was standing back listening. They'd always -- try to tell a story with your horn. Whatever you play, try to make a story out of it. Don't just go up there and blow something, you know, that you'd -- you don't know what you're doing, making a lot of noise. Say, always try to tell a little story on each thing that you play. That has always stuck by me, right until today. He said, make a little story out of it. And to present it so that the people will turn around and look and listen. Cause you can play -- you can play a solo in a place where people are drinking and eating, and they don't pay you any mind, they keep on drinking and eating and talking loud.
But you can shock them with something effective, that will make them turn around and stop, all of a sudden, and listen. That I've never forgot.
You are know, what, going into your 76th year?
I'm going into my 71st.
71st year, rather.
Yes.
But, you're playing a lot more trumpet than Louis was when -- in his last year. You know Louis was -- why was it --
Oh, yes, he wasn't playing too much.

Why is it that you are able to -- you know, to sound so young and to play so young? I mean a lot of musicians, Martin Williams just pointed out to me, think that you're somebody -- you're in your 40's.
Well, you know --
Cause you have that youthfulness about you, you have that technique which men your age, very often no longer have.

Well you see -- I think, you see you take Louis Armstrong, he travelled and he had this small band, and he a set program. That he would play all the time. His program was set. So, at his age, and travelling around, I think he tried to make it as -- he made it as easy on himself as possible by not playing anything other than his program. And when you do that then a lot of things leave you.

You take Jonah Jones is the same way. Jonah Jones, he plays one program, every night on his jobs. So there's 1,000 of things that he has forgotten. And there are many things that I don't say Louis has forgotten, but they just don't play anymore. He'll play the same program year in and year out. Earl Hines the same way. Play the same program -- if you hear Earl today, his program, maybe he'll do the same thing he did last year.
But Earl though I have heard Earl play something like, 'Caution Blues,' and 'Smashing Thirds,'
and I've heard him play it so many times, and each time it is different, though.
Different, that's right.
He does --
Well, that's that training, that's what I was telling you about --
But piano is a little different, Quite different.
Yeah, from trumpet.
From trumpet. What I mean is that, you know, you don't sound like a 70 year old man playing the trumpet, you just don't.
Well, I don't want to sound like that.
Well, of course not, but how do you do it?

Well, I do it by practicing every day, and by listening. I don't listen to -- I listen to the new trumpet players all the time. The guys that I like, as I say, Clifford Brown, I admired him and I study him, I study his records every day and I see the things that he's doing that were not done back in the '20's. And I used to -- and I listen to other trumpet players. I run into quite a few great trumpet players, say Bobby Hackett, for instance, will -- he's slowed down a little bit, but he has something and I listen to all of them. Even Benny Carter, Benny Carter and I
were great friends, you know, and I think I was responsible for Benny Carter taking up trumpet. I gave him his first mouthpiece.
Oh, you did?

I did. I gave Benny his first mouthpiece. We were with the Cotton Pickers and he was saying, I think I'm going to play trumpet. And I say, why not. He says, well, I can play the saxophone, he say, won't that affect my lip? I said, no, because I play saxophone and trumpet all the same time and I encourd him to do it. And so I gave him his first mouthpiece. And he wanted to play trumpet one day, and I said, come on and play and so he picked up his trumpet and started to play. He'll tell you the same thing today.

He always give me credit for that. Well, Benny Carter turned out to be an exceptional trumpet player. And I listen to his records, all the time; His trumpet playing. And I like Clifford Brown, as I say, he's one of my favorites and I like -- I listen to Miles Davis, a lot. The things that I understand that he's doing, I got some very nice information from his playing. And that's all I do, is sit home and listen and I play, if something hits me -- I heard something the other day, yesterday, by a trumpet player that -- who the heck was it, but I quickly wrote it down on paper, because it was -- oh, Harold Baker. I made a recording with Harold Baker, he was very nice to me to let me record with him. I thought that

was great. And I went through Kansas City with Cab's band, and he was a kid then, he sat under me, sat behind me, all the time, listening to me play, he came -- and I didn't know who he was, he said, gee I hope, I'd just love to play like that. He liked me so well, and then told me -- I made a recording with him. And he said, he told me who he was. I'd forgotten about him. He said, I used to sit there and hear me play. And he said I always wanted to play like that -- and I thought it was very nice of him to give me an opportunity to record with him because I thought he was tops, you know?

And I hear things from him. I was playing that album the other day, and some of the tunes we recorded on there, I'm playing today. And I learned a little from that -- from him, the approach that he has -- certain changes, chord changes, that I immediately write it down on paper, because it's something that I haven't done and something that I haven't heard anyone else do. And I do that every day. And I practice every day. I practice breathing, I go through tongueing, and I don't drink. I smoke a pipe a lot, but I don't drink and I try to get my rest.
I want to be fresh and I --
Well, that's what I was getting to because that explains your young ideas, your musical thinking, but I was going to ask you about the technique, you see.
Uh-huh.
So, it is practicing every day --
It's practicing every day --
and taking care of yourself --
Yes --
-- physically.

Yes. Practice every day and I find that it pays off. Now, I get through working, say, 11:00 o'clock I breakneck home, get home and go to sleep. Then I wake up early, turn my records on, and listen to all these programs, jazz, and I want to hear who's playing something. And -- you see I was thrown in -- my whole life I had a list of the trumpet players that I've played with, it would take maybe three or four hours to name the trumpet players I've played with. From Joe Smith, to Rex Stewart, to the trumpet player that did all the writing for McKenna's Cotton Pickers, I forget his name, Nesbit. All these guys were different. No two guys played alike. All up the line, Rex Stewart, I thought Rex was one of the greatest -- I never saw a man play like that, without using the proper fingering of his valves. He never used proper fingering of his valves to play anything, with any valve, it didn't make any difference to him. So, I sat under these guys all of my life and I paid attention to them. All of them, everyone of them to Arthur Whetsol, Bubba Miley, Cootie Wetzel, to Bubba Marley, Cootie, Shirley Clay, Jack Hatton, Irving Ham Davis, Reverend Randolph, gosh I could sit here and name

them all night long. But I listened to these guys, they all had something great about them. About their playing, so I wanted to be able to play with them and I did play with them and last -- night before last I played with, as I said, Clark Terry, I worked with him, played with him and the night before last I was at a seminar, I played with Thad Jones and Jimmy Owens. Now we had -- went on individually, we gave our history of what we're playing and our style of playing and so we did solo play, like I preached on the trumpet, like I used to go out on jobs because they wanted to hear me preach. On the trumpet, Now they don't do that today.

They said bring the boy that preaches, so I'd go out on a job and preach with a plunger and a mute and I put a hat on my head, some specs and I had a book like it was a bible, and that was the act that I had. And they would have me preaching. They thought that was great in Nashville, in those days. So I learned to do that. And I demonstrated that that over there the other night, about preaching and I showed them how it's done and all that stuff and then up to date -- I told them -- my style of trumpet playing, I guess, is a combination of everybody I've heard in my life.

Because I can't -- because that's just the way it happened, it just happened that way, like a thermometer, it changes with the conditions of the room. If I'm playing with a bebop band, if I go out on a job, and a guy plays sort of

bebop, I don't play the same way I would if I played with a Dixieland band. Or with a Latin band, or with Sammy Price as I'm playing now sometimes, everywhere I go it's a different band. So, it affects my playing differently, it depends on who I'm playing with. Now with Jimmy Owens and Thad Jones, well, I don't I ever played like that before in my life. Automatically, play it a different way.

Cause we all three of us had to play together. So I just wasn't playing wouldn't play Dixieland, I couldn't, I automatically went into -- tried to merge in with them. As best I could. So it comes with that. I haven't -- I think being in love with a trumpet is -- and wanting to sound good, is maybe is your answer to your question. Cause I hate to sound bad, I don't want to sound bad, I want to sound good, I want to sound strong and I want to know what I'm doing when I'm playing. I think that's the answer to it. I don't go oh a to no job tired and say I don't feel like playing today, or take three or four drinks before I get there to get myself together. I don't do that.

I go there with a feeling of let's go, let's play. That's way Wilbur liked my playing, because he said, it sets his band off -- it was a style that he wanted all the time, that's one reason he kept be cause he say, it lifted his band.
Uh-huh.
Now I had the same thing in Europe last year. I played with this band from Paris, I don't remember the -

-- they're very popular, in fact it's one of the greatest bands in France, I don't know the name of -- but I went on and did a program with them and they said, Jesus Christ, sound like Wilbur DeParis' band. You know? And I hear that all the time. After I left Benny Goodman, I played a job down to the Americana, from -- just by being with Benny Goodman, some -- I forget the name of this band, engaged me to play down there. And I played the same way all the time, but this time this guy said, Oh, many we sounded like Benny Goodman's band. Now what is that?

I can't understand that -- everywhere -- it's the same thing. I played with the Black Eagle Jazz Band three or four days ago, up in Massachusetts, and in the (unintelligible) place, and they were really -- was -- played the style of Wilbur DeParis. And they said, now we sound like Wilbur DeParis. Now what is that?
How free was that band? The Wilbur DeParis band? It seemed to -- it always seemed to me that it was fairly sort of rigid and pre-arranged.
I was -- it was rigid and pre-arranged. Everything was the same, every night. Routines were the same.
Uh-huh.

But he kept the band on its toes. He wouldn't let you let down one minute. And I liked that. I liked -- I don't want to get to the place where somebody says come on, come on, come on. I don't like that. And maybe that
helped -- answers your question. I practice everyday.
Now you listen to everything that's going on.
Yes.
And, so obviously you also are fully aware of musicians now, more and more and every -- just about every instrument except the tambourine, maybe. Employing electronic accessories --
Yes.
That happens with the trumpet, too, have you ever thought of that or what do you feel about that?

I never wanted that, I never wanted that. And when that first started -- when those things were first being used, I said, now this takes away from the natural sound of the horn. And it does something and I didn't want it. Now the other night there were two young bebop trumpet players at this concert over there and when I finished, one of them came to me, he say, you know I have an idea, I'm not going to buy this wa-wa thing, he says, I'm going to use the plunger and the mute and he looked at my little mute -- and I played this thing, cause I get the same thing, like I get -- like I hear the same thing with that, so why should I buy all this old thing, that you wa-wa with your feet, electronics? And it's true. I don't think it's natural. For you to play -- for anybody to play in the middle register and turn

on a gadget which makes you sound in a register lower. Now that's artificial. To me that's all artificial. Artificial. What kind of thing does that -- three octaves at one time going? I think it's a gimmick, I don't think it will ever -- it will ever replace natural playing.
The instrument loses its character.
It loses its character, absolutely, and it's a harsh sounding thing, it's no quality there, it's just a --

I've had the same feeling about, you know, most electronic instruments -- but then I, you know, then I start thinking about how much I enjoy listening to Charlie Christian, well there was an electronic instrument.
Well you see, you can get away with it with a guitar. I think, better than you can with a saxophone or trumpet.
Is it that or is it just that we've had it so many years, that we're now -- we've accepted it, what do you think?
No.
You don't?
No. I don't think we'll ever accept it. Not the electronics, not when it's -- because why you going to take -- you can't take it anywhere. You can't take that everywhere and all. All places.
Uh-huh.

See what I mean, they won't have it. And I think that distracts. Now for instance you're going to lose a lot of natural ability playing that thing cause now you're getting a sound and you're going to be honking on that thing. So naturally, you're going to neglect your ability to -- your solo playing. By jumping into those funny sounds that you get. Don't you think so?
Uh-huh.
Then you're going into something else altogether, so a guy ask you to play "Sweet Sue," you can't play it. You forget it. Or "Dinah," whatever you play, you forget it.
Now you spent so many, many, many years working as a section man --
Uh-huh.
-- you know and there's -- it's only really in recent years that you sort of come to the forefront as a soloist.
Uh-huh.
How does -- how does it feel, after all these years?
That's what I always wanted to do. I've always wanted to be a soloist, I never wanted to be a section man. But circumstances, you know, had a lot to do with

it, had a lot to do with it. I never wanted to be -- I was thrown in, just thrown in as a section man. But it has paid off because I've had the opportunity, as I've said before, of playing with some of the greatest trumpet players that ever lived.
But you still prefer to be the section man over being a leader and having that responsibility?
Oh, yeah, yes. Absolutely, yes. I don't wany any responsibility like that.
So, when you were with Goodman in the '60's, for instance, you -- did you ever get a chance to solo?
Yes, I got quite a lot of chances to solo in the band.
When did you first emerge as a soloist, when did people first start utilizing you as a soloist?
Well, I think in Nashville, Tennessee, I started playing solos back then.
Back then?
Yes, I didn't stick to anything else, that's all I did was playing solo.
Not featured?
Featured as a soloist? Well, I'll say with -- well I can't go to the carnival days, cause, -- I used to as a kid. Now in Nashville, the first big band that I played

with was older musicians, these musicians are musicians that would go out every year and play with circuses, and they would come back home when the circus ended for the season was over, so there were quite a lot of them older people, they were old enough to be my father. Well, they had a band there and they would play like for parades, for different things in Nashville, once in awhile and I used to play in that band. I wanted to play with that band. And we would stand on the streets and play -- give concerts in the downtown section of Nashville, and I would be there as a little, small, thin kid playing and they would throw money, the people of the town would just throw money at -- for me to be standing out there. They never heard a kid play so loud and so -- you know, make so much noise on a horn, as I. That was the thing, so I had a hat full of money, that they thought I would never stop playing, I was loud and louder than the guy playing trumpet in the band.
I've always been a loud trumpet player. And, so that was -- I was a soloist with them, they would play these marches and things and I would stand out and play the lead as a solo like, then.
Uh-huh.

Course, as I said, I wouldn't call that jazz. I didn't get into to solo jazz playing, I don't think, until let's see. Well Albert Wynn that was when -- I did -- as a saxophone player. I did a lot of solo work with him. And

Jelly Roll Jelly Roll with Teddy Rowe, Teddy Rowe was a great admirer -- he admired me quite a lot but he never got a chance to use me much. He taught me also a lot about solo playing, about half cocking the mute in the bell, now he was the originator of that. He taught me that.
Where was this?
In New York. And he --
And when was this?

-- oh, that was gosh, that -- let me see -- that was after -- was that after? That was during the time of the Rhythm Club, I have to pinpoint that year. The Rhythm Club was in its heyday then, they had moved -- moved from -- it was on 32nd Street, 30 something street, and there was a guy named Hall that came from Chicago, to open the Rhythm Club, George Hall, I think that was his name, he was a bass player. Did you ever hear of his name? But, he opened the Rhythm Club here in New York.

That was the time I met Jelly Roll -- in fact, if I can get back to that year, I think that was, -- that was during the time before I went to Europe with Sam Wooding. Something around in that area, in that time. Because he was still -- cussing out Melrose --
The early '20's, then?
Yes, he was still cussing out Melrose at that time. And I was supposed to record -- I made a record-

ing with Jelly Roll I don't know what it was but he took me in, he liked me and he taught me how to -- I was sitting -- I was the only trumpet player that was sitting listening to him, and that's why he liked me --
And you make recording for --

I made a recording with Jelly Roll, right here in New York. I don't know what it was because I wasn't here to long. I was in and out, running with this group, and running with that group, and being young, I didn't pay too much attention to Jelly Roll, I just knew him and he knew me and I didn't --
What were you playing, what instrument?

Trumpet. I didn't know that he was one day going to become, you know, famous. I knew he was -- he sat down and played his whole -- every tune he ever wrote, he sat down and played for me, one day. All his shouts and everything, 'Pearls' and everything, he said I wrote all this, he said, I'm the greatest, I did this, these things -- he played for me, gave me a concert one day. He wouldn't do things like that.
Well, he did, really, pioneer a lot of --
He absolutely did but I didn't realize that at that time.
Uh-huh.

But I've always the person that would sit down and listen, I'm not going to give a man a hard time. Now, so Jolly Roll Sewell General gave me an opportunity to solo. Now, they came up into Sam Woodings band and when I went with -- to Europe with Sam, I was a lead trumpet player, but when Tommy left, I played all of Tommy's solos. In the band, and so that was the beginning of -- also it came gradual, cause I was in between playing lead trumpet, and solo, it came slowly, cause I worked with a fellow in New York named Billy Butler, he was the guy that wrote this travel guide, he was a concert director.

And he had the band when I worked for the Cavalcade of Broadway, Ed Sullivan's show, that the first broadway show that I played. Bill Butler directed the band, there. And I also played some gigs with him.
This was when?
That was, oh, gosh, that was in the '30's. Sometime in there. That was when Tim Moore was the comedian on the show. Tim Moore, you don't remember --
Tim and Gertie Moore. Yeah.
No, Tim Moore was a --
Amos and Andy.
That's right.
Right.
Now Billy Butler was gigging around

town, he had a lot of gigs. He would carry me. Renauld Jones was with -- he and I worked with -- Billy Butler would never let me play a solo. He said, no you're a lead trumpet player. Never a solo. One day I played a solo and -- on "Hallelujah" and he said, no, no, no, no. He waved his hands at me and I didn't pay him no mind because I knew what I played was right. But he never wanted me to play a solo. So I think, actually, Cab gave me a few -- quite a lot of solos, but they were nice, pretty things, like "World on a String," and "Cabin in the Cotton," but he would never let me shout on my horn. Cause he had Swazee there, he had Randolph, he had Lamar Wright to do it.

But I played mostly all of his beautiful solos, "Nagasaki," I think he turned me loose a couple of times on that. But he never regarded me as a jazz soloist, but as a lead man I played pretty solos. That's what Cab --
(More) Straight things?
Yeah.
But now you've written a book on improvisation.

I did that, yes, because I wanted to do it. I wanted to express myself some kind of way, so I did it in book form and Wilbur DeParis turned me loose as a soloist. I had free hand and that's what I like. I think he really gave me the more opportunity than anyone.
Uh-huh.

To play solos. Cause Wilbur, a guy that he didn't care if your solo was bad, he wouldn't even say a thing about it, he would let you go right ahead, he always had confidence in his men, to know that if they make a mistake, if they do bad one day, the next day they'd be better. That's the way he was, he gave me all the opportunity to -- in the world. And whenever I'd go to Europe, I'd always go there as a soloist, not as a lead man, they always gave me a chance in Europe as a soloist and I wanted to be a soloist, I didn't want to be a lead man, but that's the thing that hurt me.

I was with George Weir, I played -- I was with Vic up there I did all the solo work. I was getting together, you know, and then you jump in the Latin band as a soloist, then you come out of there and you get it so I just made up my mind that I'm going to stay away from the Latin music, as much as possible. I hope. And stay with this so I could kind of get my mind together -- you know, back to where I want to be. I don't know what's happening. I -- everything seems to be working out all right.
Well, when will Doc Cheatham retire?

Well, I guess the day that I can't play another note. That'll be the day. Because I still like playing and I'm going to play as long as I can -- as long as I have the wind. And the teeth, and if the teeth go before the wind, then I'll go downtown, down to Nashville, my brother's

a great surgeon-dentist, and he'll make me a set of teeth, and I will we'll try to continue, cause I think you can play with false teeth and you can play without teeth. I've known trumpet players to play without teeth. As long as my health holds up, I'm going to play because I like it, I don't see nothing else to do.
What about composing?

No, I never wanted to compose. I never had a desire to compose, never had a desire, I wrote a couple of tunes, but they were lousy. And I just forgot about it. I'm not a composer. But I like challenges, I like to be thrown in, with fast company, you know, all the time, I like that --
Uh-huh.
Just like that in Nice, I was thrown up there with Clark Terry, I felt very honored, but I wanted to. I wanted him to make me play, and he made me play. I have the tape of that.
You ever play the flugel horn?

No, I don't have the desire to play the flugel horn. I don't think -- to me, I like to hear the guys play it, but it's not a trumpet, no you can't compare with a trumpet, in no way. Sound of it is different, and it takes away from your trumpet playing. Because it's a deeper instru- ment. And if you're not careful, you will lose your lip for

the trumpet. So a lot of the trumpet players who switched to the flugel horn play flugel horn all the time, because it's a different pressure. It's a different pressure and it's easier, than a trumpet.
Are there any young trumpet players, today, whom you admire particularly? Up and coming people?
Well no, I don't think so. Yes, one, there's a kind by the name of Vache, Warren Vache.
I've never heard of him.
Oh, he's with Goodman, he does things like with Goodman, now. Concerts. He's a newcomer, I like --
Yeah?

-- I like him very much. Cause he's doing the things -- he did the things that we used to do. He goes around and sits in with all of us. He comes over -- he came over where I played in Jersey, almost every week and bring his horn and get on the bandstand and we jammed together, we played together.
How do you spell his name?
V-a-c-h-e. Warren Vache.
Vache.
Yeah, he goes around, that's what he did and he's developed into a great trumpet player.
What about John Faldis?
Yes, I'm glad you've mentioned his

name, yes. I admire John Faddis Davis, I admire him very much. He's got -- he has a will to play and that's what you need. He's got that will, he's going to be -- he's going to be one of the -- just about the top trumpet player of the day, if some other kid don't come along and out-grow low him. Cause he's got the will and the determination to be a discipline -- just about the top trumpet player and you're going to see that.
Well he's a great admirer, of course, of Dizzy.
Oh, and Miles Davis. Well you could tell that in his playing.
Uh-huh.
You could tell that in his playing. He has awhile to go, but if he just -- if nothing detracts his attention, he'll make it right straight to the top.
Do you like what Miles is doing these days?

Some of it yes, yes. I listen to Miles things. I get something out of his. There's something I can get out of everybody. All trumpet players, a little something. I get a lot of things from Miles. Maybe that the ordinary person, listening, would overlook, it'll just go through one ear and out the other.
Uh-huh.
But you have to dig down into the

bowels of the -- of what these guys are doing. To get -- see what they're trying -- they know what they're doing. They know what they're trying to do and they know where -- so many of us will not understand it, will not get it. But I listen to Miles, I've always listened to Miles. And I get something out of his -- in fact Herbie Mann told me one day, and -- in Dakar, Africa, we were rehearsing and I was playing like Miles, and he said you sound like Miles Davis. I got a big kick out of it, because I can imitate Miles to a certain extent, a little bit, I can. And I think there's something I get out of him, out of all trumpet players, Miles and everybody else.
Uh-huh.
And one guy I like very much, what was his name, he was killed, down in the Village, shot, what was his name?
Kenny Durham?
No.
Oh, oh, I know who you're talking about, he was shot at Art Slugs.
Yeah. I did -- I admired that guy. His playing.
Uh-huh.
And I'm sorry what happened to him, I didn't get a chance to see him more often. But I listened to a lot of his recordings. He's great. And Fats Navarro and
Lee Morgan.
Lee Morgan.
Uh-huh.

Yeah. I get something out of those guys and I think it's important. Because you can't put them down, unless you know what you're putting them down for. Of course, Dizzy, too. Dizzy -- get a big kick out of him.
He's got a great sense of humor.

Yes, he has. So, all in all, I think that I think I have had the pleasure of playing with more trumpet players than most all of those boys. Cause I came up all the way from Buddy Lee to -- there's another guy that you probably never heard of, Buddy Lee was a great trumpet player.
Yeah.

He was the first high note trumpet player I ever heard in my life. And I think he was just about the first -- to high note trumpet player that came along, that could play high-C then, was something to play.
This was in Nashville?
No, this was in Detroit, he was with the Cotton Pickers before I joined them then.
Oh, oh, right.
First one that I heard play a high-C.
So that was in the '30's, early '30's
you heard him?
Yes, yes. Then we go to Nesbit, that's a guy that you don't hear much about.
Yeah, yeah.

Those guys were great trumpet players. And you see you get a little something from everybody that just automatically you just -- you just -- I guess absorb a lot of things, a lot of styles into -- and before you know it, you have a style of your own. That comes -- that comes -- I always did like a lot of attack. I've always liked that -- that's what I got from Bix Beiderbecke. I think Bix Beiderbecke had the greatest attack for playing jazz of any trumpet player.

Now don't -- Louie didn't have all that attack, he didn't need it, he didn't want it, because he was a different approach and Bix had an attack, that I liked and I think I still have that attack. Cause I like it because it -- it -- immediately attracts attention, you know, I do it every night a lot of times before I blast last night I played it all night long -- an attack like that and people turn around and everybody coming up there. You know? It's important. And I think if you're doing something, do it so somebody knows that you're doing it. Everybody knows you're doing it.
In other words if I were to ask you who influenced you we'd have another hour.
We would have more than an hour. Cause
I left out a lot of guys, you know.
Uh-huh.
I've omitted a lot of guys. Because it's as I say, I'm going to play until I drop. I mean if I have a heart attack then I'll stop cause I think that's the time to stop.
Right.
As long as my heart's good and my teeth, my lungs are good, I'm going to continue to play. Because I still like it.
Great. Well thank you.
Okay.
(End of proceedings.)
